subtopic: DIVERSION OF CANADIAN WHEAT AND FLOUR BY RUSSIA TO CUBA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I direct this question to the Prime Minister because the matter covers more than one department. It has to do with an article in the London Sunday Times of yesterday's date regarding the diversion by the U.S.S.R. of wheat sold under the contract between the U.S.S.R. and the Canadian wheat board. Is it a fact that some 250,000 tons of wheat and flour under the 1963 contract with the U.S.S.R. were diverted by the purchaser, the U.S.S.R., to Cuba; and was this action agreed to by the Canadian government? Naturally I should like to know too whether the wheat board asked for the views of the Canadian government before consenting to this diversion.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: DIVERSION OF CANADIAN WHEAT AND FLOUR BY RUSSIA TO CUBA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did notice the report to which my right hon. friend has referred, and I am going to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce to deal with the matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: DIVERSION OF CANADIAN WHEAT AND FLOUR BY RUSSIA TO CUBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members may recall from my disclosure to the house last year of the terms of the agreement between the U.S.S.R., the Canadian government and the Canadian wheat board, there were in effect two agreements, one of them under which the U.S.S.R. purchased certain quantities of wheat and flour on which credit terms were available, and a second agreement relating to the sale of wheat and flour for Cuba. Under that second part of the agreement sales were strictly for cash.
To make the position quite clear, Mr. Speaker, under the Canada-U.S.S.R. trade agreement concluded last fall there was a 20220-453i
Inquiries of the Ministry sale of approximately 252,000 tons of wheat and 175,000 tons of flour for direct shipment to Cuba on a cash basis. I might add that all shipments of wheat and flour purchased under the Canada-U.S.S.R. wheat agreement have been completed with the exception of a small quantity of flour to be delivered shortly to Cuba.

subtopic: DIVERSION OF CANADIAN WHEAT AND FLOUR BY RUSSIA TO CUBA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would then direct this question to the Prime Minister. With respect to the diversion of this wheat and flour to Cuba, has there been any complaint made by any friendly government?

subtopic: DIVERSION OF CANADIAN WHEAT AND FLOUR BY RUSSIA TO CUBA
speechtext: Not to my knowledge, Mr. Speaker; and even those governments which have cut off normal trade with Cuba have agreed, I think-I am speaking particularly of the United States-not to prevent the sale to Cuba for cash of exports of certain foodstuffs and medical supplies.

subtopic: DIVERSION OF CANADIAN WHEAT AND FLOUR BY RUSSIA TO CUBA

subtopic: DIVERSION OF CANADIAN WHEAT AND FLOUR BY RUSSIA TO CUBA

I want to ask the Prime Minister a question. It arises from a speech by Dr. Deutsch which was widely reported in the United States. speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):

speechtext: I would be very glad to discuss the matter with Dr. Deutsch and see whether the text of that speech can be made available to members.

The house resumed, from Thursday, August 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson:
That the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to establish officially as the flag of Canada a flag embodying the emblem proclaimed by His Majesty King George V on November 21, 1921-three maple leaves conjoined on one stem-in the colours red and white then designated for Canada, the red leaves occupying a field of white between vertical sections of blue on the edges of the flag.
And the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. More.

Mr. Speaker, on Thursday I referred to the introduction of this flag resolution and to the Prime Minister's open invitation to members to participate. It is a well known fact that members on this side of the house have since accepted that invitation and have made their observations on this subject. The Prime Minister saw fit on one occasion to refer to this as a filibuster. Whether the participation to which I have referred is known as a filibuster or not, I can tell the house that I personally am proud to take part in this debate.
When I spoke on Thursday I also gave reasons why I personally believe that the term "filibuster" as applied by the Liberals to the debate is certainly not applicable to what has taken place in this house. I indicated that in Wednesday's debate, which took up fewer than 29 pages of Hansard, there were two pages of rulings from the Chair, 61 identified interruptions and in all more than 100 interjections by hon. members. There were, in addition, speeches by an hon. member of the New Democratic party and by a representative of "the Liberal group", to repeat a phrase used by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the course of his own contribution, during which he made no reference whatsoever to his leader, or to the Liberals being a party.
This reminds one of the statement made by the Minister of Finance during a television broadcast when he said he "thought the Liberal party had a leader." In this case the Minister of Trade and Commerce does not

recognize that there is either a party or a leader. Of course, as was mentioned on another occasion, the hon. gentleman has his own ambitions and is probably directing all his energies in that direction.
The Minister of Forestry took exception to certain remarks I was making and rose to tell the house just why he was present as a minister. It is interesting to see that as reported on page 7106 of Hansard, in the second column, the minister's first sentence was:
I thought we had been elected in this parliament to take decisions.
This fact is clearly indicated by the Liberal party when it takes the decision, the personal decision, of the Prime Minister and gives it its blessings. It has been my understanding that we as members are here to make decisions. Of course it is a very simple matter to make a decision, but it is our further duty to make the right decision. Much doubt has been cast on the decision of this house to introduce to this country a three maple leaves flag which is the personal choice of the Prime Minister.
I say it is his personal choice, Mr. Speaker, because in my own province, as I said before, the two members for Halifax, in my opinion with prior knowledge, made these very bold statements which are a clear indication to the Prime Minister that his personal choice has not been accepted within his own party. These two hon. members made it quite clear that any support which they would give the three maple leaves flag was qualified support.
I further indicated, Mr. Speaker, that the members of his own cabinet are divided on this particular matter, and I threw out the challenge that one particular minister had informed me that his choice would be anything but the three maple leaves flag. He was against it. At the same time he indicated to me what was his choice, which is a clear-cut indication that within the cabinet itself this party is divided. And why should it not be divided? It is the personal selection of the Prime Minister. The Minister of Forestry indicated that we were here to take decisions, but hon. gentlemen opposite are giving the decision of	the Prime Minister their
blessing.
Why have we not heard from the Liberal members on this particular matter, Mr. Speaker? Why do they not get up in support of the three maple leaves flag? Why have we not heard from the two members for Halifax, who qualified their support for the three maple leaves flag? Let us hear them get up now and give their unqualified support. Let us also hear from the cabinet minister who is
Canadian Flag
quite dissatisfied with this proposed flag. These opinions were all expressed prior to the introduction of this resolution, so let us hear these hon. gentlemen support the three maple leaves flag; and give it unqualified support, not the qualified support they indicated they would give when they knew what the resolution would contain.

I would not support your
filibuster.
They have nothing to say.
The hon. member now interjecting is well aware of what I think of his ability, especially when he was trying to chair a certain committee.
Which member?

He does not even show enough ability to make himself properly identifiable. The finger of blame in this debate has been pointed in many directions and for many reasons, but as far as I am concerned the finger can only be pointed in one direction, and that is in the direction of the Prime Minister himself, who has made a personal choice and imposed it on the members of his party. Perhaps I should say "group", because after all that is what the Minister of Trade and Commerce called it. He has imposed on his own group his opinion of what should be the flag design.
The Prime Minister has now said that he is willing to allow this matter to go before a committee. This was the suggestion put forward some time ago by the Leader of the Opposition. However, the Prime Minister's willingness to allow it to go to a committee comes rather late, considering that his action to date has put his own members in such a position that they are more or less obligated to go along with the pressure put upon them by the Prime Minister, which was made quite clear when he introduced his resolution in the first place.
I say the finger can be pointed in one direction and one direction only, namely directly at the Prime Minister. Should he not wish to take my word for this, perhaps he would like to go back to some of the advisers he was looking to for advice not too long ago. He might question the advice of Mr. Ryan of he Devoir, to whom I understand he went for advice. He might ask what Mr. Ryan thinks of this particular flag design; and in that connection he might read an editorial which appeared in that paper over the week end in which the lack of leadership on his part in pointed out, a matter which his own group is fully realizing is the case today.

Canadian Flag
Question.

Mr. Speaker, the usual sort of contribution is coming from hon. members opposite. I have invited them to get up, if they are in favour of the three maple leaves flag, and give the house their unqualified support for the personal choice of the Prime Minister. But that they cannot do.
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. I submit that the fairy tales told by the hon. member in the last ten minutes have nothing to do with the subamendment and should be ruled out of order.

I have been listening intently to the speech of the hon. member, and frequently during the last few minutes he has referred to the question of designs. There was the question of the three maple leaves and of one or two other designs alluded to by the subamendment. In my opinion, although he is being rather general he is within the ambit of the subamendment.

Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to you for putting the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Regan) in his place. However, through you, sir, I would call his attention to the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, his own colleague, to which he did not see fit to rise and raise a point of order. If I have strayed I submit I have not strayed nearly as far as did the hon. member's own colleague, the minister, on that occasion.
With reference to the three leaves design, it has become obvious across the country to many members of the Liberal group that what the Prime Minister has tried to do in foisting his personal choice upon this parliament has become a very difficult task, and quite possibly hon. gentlemen opposite will rise in their places within the next few hours or days and those who can will indicate their reasons for supporting the three maple leaves flag. But I would very much doubt whether many of them could do that with a clear conscience.
Today we have a flag flying which was referred to by the late Mackenzie King as the official Canadian flag. We have flying today a flag which was recognized by Prime Minister Louis St. Laurent, who said that no new flag should be a party flag. We have flying today a flag which was recognized by the present Leader of the Opposition when he was prime minister. In conclusion I can only say that if it was good enough for the three prime ministers prior to this administration coming into office, it is certainly good enough 
for this present Prime Minister leading the group he is in in this house.
The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to be recognized even though I have not yet risen. Perhaps I might attribute my recognition to the shadow cast by my six foot five inch frame when I do rise. This reminds me of the situation one found, as a small boy born in the days before there was complete pollution of our streams, before our rivers were dammed and all the brooks had been frozen, when one walked along the banks of a brook in late February or early March and heard the sound of a little water trickling underneath the ice. Then one could run back home and say "I think, spring is coming". Sometimes, of course, spring was followed by a freeze and the water would stop running. Sometimes the water kept on running and it would not be too long before one could hear the cracking and booming of the ice in the lakes and would know that a complete thaw had taken place; that not only had spring arrived but summer, even a belated one, was not far removed.
Certainly this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I am speaking in an atmosphere similar to that sound of running water underneath the ice, and at this stage I should not want to say anything or do anything which would result in a freeze and stop the running of the water. We can always be optimistic, and perhaps it behooves all of us at this time to be very careful of the situation.
Mr. Speaker, there are one or two general statements I should like to make while carrying on this debate. In the first place I think all members here are fair minded, subject to some political pressure, and will admit that this debate has been of a very high standard.
Oh, oh.

Did I hear something from the other side? I might have known that some would disagree.
This has been an emotionally charged debate in respect of matters which are very close to many of the members. This is a debate which could have aroused bitter feelings, recriminations and statements which would be very difficult to overlook or control in a parliament such as this. Of course there have been political overtones, as there always are when dealing with matters of this kind; because in a proper sense of the word this

is a political body, and politics are bound to be interspersed in our activities.
I do suggest there have been less politics and more sentiment and expression of feeling during this debate, considering the subject matter. I am sure that students of parliamentary history, when reading the speeches made during this debate at some time in the future when many of us are no longer members here, will find it very difficult to understand the comments of some of the press columnists to the effect that this is a very poor parliament. A poor parliament could not have produced a debate such as we have had, and I refer to speeches made by hon. members on all sides of this house. Some great speeches have been made. Of course all the speeches made have not been great, but on the whole parliament as an institution can be very proud of the debate which has taken place.
As I have said, I am sure that students in the future, after we have been long since forgotten individually, will read this debate not only to discover the history of Canada but because of its high quality. The speeches have been emotionally charged, but the situation has been adequately handled. I am sure speeches to be made from now on will continue to be of that high order.
Mr. Speaker, there are two misconceptions I should like to deal with at this time. One has been the suggestion that this debate is a filibuster. That suggestion has been made casually by one or two hon. members opposite, although not by those in the front row. That suggestion has been mentioned casually on occasion by the radio and press men. The suggestion was given an official position a day or two ago by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who referred to the debate as a Tory filibuster. That was the first time the expression was used by an hon. gentleman in the front row opposite. That minister had the nerve and temerity to call this a Tory filibuster.
I remind that hon. gentleman that we are speaking here today at the proper request of the Prime Minister, who said it was the duty and responsibility of all hon. members in all parties to not only express the feelings of their constituents but their own feelings as well. I agree with the Prime Minister that it is our duty to express our opinions, and that is exactly what we are doing and have been doing for a week or more. It is true that one or two speeches have been made in repetition, and that two or three 20220-454
Canadian Flag
speakers have spoken twice during this debate. That is understandable for various reasons known to hon. members who have had the responsibility of marshalling the debate and arranging for speakers.
Generally speaking there has been no repetition. This is the first time I have spoken during this debate, and I know there are other members on this side of the house who have not spoken but who will, I am sure, take part in this debate. They will not be taking part in a Tory filibuster but will be expressing their opinions in response to the wishes of their constituents. Our constituents expect us to speak, Mr. Speaker, and for some of us in any event our consciences demand that we do so. I think in all fairness that fact is generally recognized by hon. members on the other side of the house.
Mr. Speaker, I think there has been a little suggestion, outside those one or two references by hon. members opposite who criticize us because we are taking up some time, that this is in fact a filibuster. There has been some criticism on the part of radio commentators and editorial writers who suggest this debate is being carried on for purely political purposes and that we are speaking only for the benefit of the people back home. All I can say, Mr. Speaker, is that these intellectual halfwits who have no knowledge of sentiment or emotion themselves are hardly in a position to speak for those of us who do feel keenly and strongly about this matter.
If anyone desires a political reply to the charge of filibuster, Mr. Speaker, I call upon that distinguished member of the press gallery, Mr. Blair Fraser, who has never been recognized as a Conservative apologist but who has been accused of writing apologia for the Liberal party. He is a personal friend of mine, and I absolve him of that latter charge entirely. Mr. Fraser several days ago, commenting over C.B.C., said this was one of a number of false statements being put forward by certain people. He wanted to deny emphatically that it was the purpose of the Conservative spokesmen in the House of Commons, who were exercising their rights, to conduct a filibuster.
The second misconception, Mr. Speaker, is related to the suggestion that we are blocking or interfering with the nation's business. I must say that we are very concerned with the nation's business. I remind hon. members that the Prime Minister outlined the business which had to be done before the flag debate commenced and suggested that after the flag

Canadian Flag
debate was concluded there was going to be a recess of parliament. The business to which the right hon. Prime Minister referred has been completed and we are now dealing with the flag debate. If we are interfering with anything, Mr. Speaker, apparently we are interfering with our own vacations. There may be those who think we do not deserve to have a vacation because we are now receiving the huge sum of $18,000 a year. In any event, no one could suggest we are blocking the nation's business, because we would be away from this place were it not for this particular debate.
I think all members of parliament, not only those on this side, have been subject to a very caustic and critical press because of the fact they are prepared to participate in and listen to this debate when, were it not for this debate, they would be out of here. Again, if one wants to call an unprejudiced witness, in that same radio broadcast to which I referred a few moments ago Mr. Blair Fraser said no one could accuse the Conservative opposition of interfering with or interrupting the business of the country because if we were not dealing with this issue we would be away on our vacation and the business of the country would not be under discussion.

The government has
nothing ready.

The Leader of the Opposition says the government has nothing ready. We are at least giving them time in which to produce something. We hope that when we get through with this matter they will be able to produce something, and if they do we will deal with it.
I wish to make one further reference to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. We all appreciate the real and obviously sincere concern which he felt for the future of the Conservative party. It almost brought tears to our eyes to realize he was so concerned about our future and, as I said, we appreciate it. But I will tell him that having been here for quite a few years and having taken part in public life in this country for many years, I have a very high appreciation of the contribution the Liberal party has made to the history and development of this nation, and I appreciate the fact that the Minister of Trade and Commerce shares these views and recognizes the countribution which the Conservative party has made to the history and development of this country.
With all due respect to hon. members farther down this side of the house and the

contributions they have made from time to time for the good of the nation, I think everyone realizes that the two great old parties have been largely responsible for the development of Canada, and I hope and expect that this will continue to be so. But I want to assure the Minister of Trade and Commerce that his worry about our future is no greater than our worry about their future. What we are afraid of is that the Liberal party, as a result of their actions in this debate and the attitude they have taken, are going to become a sectional party rather than a national party and will largely cease to exist in certain parts of the country.
On Friday the Prime Minister made a statement which was very belated but very welcome. Apparently when the votes are taken on the amendments and the motion before the house the party whips will be relaxed and hon. members may vote as they see fit. This is certainly a rather belated conversion. As I have said, I do not want to deaden the sound of running water and I certainly do not want to raise any blood pressures at this time, but I think anybody will admit that the action of the government in bringing forward the flag resolution and the way it has been handled has been characterized, to put it gently and kindly, by a certain degree of stupidity and a high degree of stubbornness. No more kindly description could be applied to what has happened.
We were told that a flag had been produced by somebody for which the Prime Minister apparently took credit, although most of those on the other side do not know who produced it; and we were told that we could take it or leave it and if we did not take it there would be an election. If ever before there has been a political blunder in a highly emotional situation such as this, I have never seen it. I doubt that there ever has been such an action since confederation which affected people generally in their hearts, their souls and their minds to the extent this has, and which has been characterized with such stubbornness and such stupidity as the government has shown up to now. Therefore we welcome the statement of the Prime Minister that there will be no political pressure brought to bear on hon. members opposite when we come to vote, in that the whips will be off and the fate of the government will not be determined in any way, shape or form. In other words there is not going to be an election-
Three months late.

-because of the result of the vote. In that connection I draw attention to a former political leader in this house who was succeeded by an hon. gentleman to my left. I refer to Hon. M. J. Coldwell who was leader of the C.C.F. party in years gone by and who is one of the distinguished parliamentarians of this parliament and country. I wish to quote from a speech he made in the house on December 9, 1953. As found on page 748 of Hansard, he said:
No partisan recommendation should be made. When a recommendation is made to parliament-
He was referring to a flag.
-the government should feel that it would be acceptable at least to the vast majority of members in all parts of the house. The matter of choosing a national emblem is too important to have connected with it any sort of political controversy either In the house or across the country.
Those words, uttered in 1953 by one of the distinguished parliamentarians of this country and of this century, are words which 1 would commend to all hon. members at this time. As I say, we welcome this conversion on the part of the Prime Minister, belated though it is. Some of us cannot quite forget the communist trials in the Stalin era when men were so brainwashed while they were confined that when they were released and brought into the open courtroom they confessed to sins of which they had never heard because they had been brainwashed to that extent. I hope that the brainwashing which has taken place on the other side of the house has not been of such severity and intensity that hon. members opposite cannot recover from it before we come to the vote.
1 see that time is passing, Mr. Speaker, and as I did not mark the time I started I must watch myself. A partisan decision as to the flag was the first mistake that was made by the government. The second mistake which I suggest has been made by the government in dealing with this matter was when the proposed flag brought forward by the Prime Minister and the government was denuded of all historical significance, of everything which bespeaks our pride, our history and our traditions.
I have heard it said that the red ensign does not have a great deal of history behind it. There has been debate as to when it was used first. It has been said that it was flown over the parliament buildings up to 1904 and that it was then taken down. I have heard it suggested that it was not used during the first world war and that it came into use by virtue of some order in council long after the first world war was over.

I can speak with some little authority in this matter because I happen to be one who as a very junior soldier served in France for a very short time during the first world war. I well remember Sir Robert Borden, for instance, then prime minister of Canada, coming to Tincques in France on July 1, 1918, Dominion day, and Canadian ensigns were flying to welcome the prime minister. I am sure that others in the house including the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre who served in the first world war, can vouch for the statement I am making today.
If one wants further corroboration one does not need to go to a Tory politician or spokesman. I would refer the house to General Andrew McNaughton, who could hardly be described as a Tory supporter. I have been talking to him lately. He was commander of the Canadian corps of artillery during the first world war and was a great soldier and a great leader in the field. He said that the Canadian red ensign flew over the corps headquarters at that time. He remembers it very well, and he was proud of the fact that it was there.
May I ask a question on that point? Was it not the blue ensign? Was not General Currie's flag the blue ensign?

I am not sure what General Currie's flag may have been. General Currie was commander of the Canadian corps, which was almost equivalent to an army command, although it was only recognized as a corps. General Currie may have had his own flag and it may have been the blue ensign. However, so far as the Canadian corps troops were concerned, so far as the Canadians serving in France were concerned, it was the red ensign that was flying.
As I have said, I think the second mistake which was made in connection with this proposed flag was the denuding from it of all references to our tradition, our pride and our history. You are taking a flag which is rich in history, which is colourful, and discarding it. I remember the first day I came into the courtyard of this House of Commons. Perhaps to some extent I was emotionally aroused because I was taking a seat in the House of Commons. However, I have never forgotten the picture of that red ensign flying over the peace tower. I never can forget it. I can say, and I am sure most hon. members will agree with me, that in colour, in richness and in the general picture that

Canadian Flag
this flag presents, it is second to none which is flying anywhere in the world today.
Now, it the resolution is adopted we are starting literally-and I do not mean to make a pun-and figuratively with a clean sheet. We are going to do away with our history and our tradition. In that connection I should like to refer the right hon. Prime Minister and other Liberals to the statement of a great liberal-not Liberal in the political sense-President Woodrow Wilson. We all recognize him as one of the great liberals of the North American continent. He said this in an address on June 14, 1915:
The things that the flag stands for were created by the experiences of a great people. Everything that it stands for was written by their lives. The flag is the embodiment, not of sentiment, but of history. It represents the experiences made by men and women, the experiences of those who do and live under that flag.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that is as fair a definition of a flag as one can get, and I commend it to hon. gentlemen opposite. The corollary to that mistake is the belief that the Canadian people would accept this denuding of our flag, this stripping of our heritage and tradition. There has never been a greater example, I will not say of political stupidity but of political ignorance, than has been shown in connection with this matter; to think that the Canadian people would stand idly by and see the flag which millions revere being cast aside so that we start off again with a clean sheet. If any government thought that would be accepted by the Canadian people, it is absolutely beyond my comprehension.
The reason for it, of course, or so we are told, is that this will achieve national unity. Feeling strongly as I do on this matter, and I know I am speaking for many others who feel the same way, I may say that if by throwing our flag into discard, by coming up with a new emblem of some kind or other, we could achieve national unity; if we were convinced of that, I think we would pay that price to achieve national unity. The trouble is you hear statements made by hon. members around this building. I am not referring to any one group or province or anything else, but we hear that this will not achieve national unity. The flag is only the beginning. Our problems are much deeper, and unless other solutions, financial, constitutional and otherwise are found, national unity will not be achieved. Finally you are told that this

flag is simply a problem for English Canadians. Now, when you are facing that situation it is rather difficult to be convinced that if you are prepared to drop the red ensign, if you are prepared to start with a new sheet, you are going to achieve national unity.
We are asked to give up everything, many of us are, which we hold dear; everything of our pride, our history and our traditions. We are told afterward that this does not achieve anything in the end. Are we to scrap the flag we have, the flag which is flying over this building today, that warm, colourful, beautiful symbol of our history and our heritage? What are we to accept in exchange? We are prepared to make an exchange if we were sure it would be the means of accomplishing national unity, but we are not prepared to do it on the information we have at the moment.
We are asked to swap, and for what? We have a suggestion brought forward by the Prime Minister-I am not saying he developed it, but it is reported that he did- concerning the three maple leaf design. I had someone check with the office of the Secretary of State, and I found that there were 24 different copyrights on the three maple leaf design. They cover everything from beer to boloney and many other products in between. There are those who suggest one maple leaf as the design. I do not want to cause any discomfiture in that particular quarter, but I found that there were 327 copyrights issued covering one maple leaf. These are the matters which we are supposed to debate. We are asked to strip the hallmarks of our history and accept a copyright design for beer.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we are told that all this will achieve national unity, but I doubt it. There are extremists in all places; there are extremists both English and French. There are extremists in various provinces. We all have to recognize that fact. I recognize it, and I make apologies for some of the English speaking extremists just as I am sure some of my hon. friends from Quebec make apologies for some of the extremists in their own province. A country which has no pride in history has very little hope for posterity. I am sure the French Canadians have pride in their ancestry, just as we have in ours. I am wondering what the habitants who came to the defence of this country and fought under the union jack to defeat Montgomery and save this country from becoming a colony of the United States would think today. I would think they would turn over in

their graves if they heard some of the statements which are allegedly being made by their descendants in this country.
It is not only limited to Quebec. I am speaking now from a prejudiced, personal position. I come from the ancient province of Nova Scotia. I come from that most ancient of constituencies, Digby-Annapolis-Kings, which includes Port Royal, the ancient capital of this country. This is the place to which Champlain came. He settled in that rich valley and developed enough courage and strength during two or three years to go on and establish French settlements at Stada-cona and Hochelaga. We have a Port Royal, which name was changed only a few years ago by commission from the postmaster general in order to re-establish that old name. In that little community you have the Order of Good Cheer, which has been going on for over 300 years and which was established by Champlain. It is meeting regularly now and has been for more than three centuries. Surely this is part of our heritage, part of our tradition. One can say it has not got much to do with the flag, that you don't get a kettle on a flag; but if you scrap your traditions, if you start scrapping one then scrap all the others.
I simply point out that we have a French Canadian heritage not only in the province of Quebec, of which all Canada is proud, but we have it in my own constituency, in my own town, Port Royal. We are very proud of it, and we want to see it maintained.
My own position-and the Prime Minister said we should make our own positions clear -is very simple. In the two or three minutes left to me I want to say that in the first place I believe in supporting the red ensign. I believe it is a beautiful flag, a flag of history which contains our heritage and our traditions. I will support it as long as that is feasible in this discussion.
Hear, hear.

Some modifications may be developed. I can think of modifications which can be developed following suggestions which may be coming forward with respect to one maple leaf. Somebody said to me today, "I thought you and your party were in favour of a distinctive Canadian flag. Why have you been telling the people you are in favour of a distinctive Canadian flag if you don't intend to support the maple leaves flag?" For years my party has stated it has been in favour of a distinctive Canadian flag, but I never dreamt that by adopting a distinctive

Canadian flag we would denude it of everything of our history, traditions and heritage. I thought it would be possible with the red ensign to superimpose a maple leaf, or any other emblem, but I never thought the proposal meant the elimination of everything pertaining to our pride, history and traditions. That is what I meant, and that is what I believe my party meant when we said we were in favour of a distinctive Canadian flag.
Providing these ancient hallmarks are preserved we are prepared to accept any modification, maintaining the red ensign substantially; but I am not married to that. If that is impossible, if we cannot do that by agreement in this house, I support the proposal for a plebiscite because I believe, sir, in this matter-

As I said, Mr. Speaker, if necessary I am prepared to accept a plebiscite on this matter. I do not think it is necessary, but certainly it is better to have that, to have all the Canadian people consulted, than to have any decision forced upon us by any government majority. Or as an alternative, as the Prime Minister hinted on Friday and as the Leader of the Opposition has also mentioned, the question of a committee of the house, should be given very careful consideration if that is the only avenue possible.
I read in the paper, or heard something this morning, to the effect that "this man Diefen-baker" would not agree to a committee and that he wanted interminable debate thereon. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that for any committee which may be set up there would have to be ground rules established first, and as I understand our rules, ordinarily a majority report is printed and there is no minority report. I do not think anyone in this parliament would expect a committee to be set up which would simply bring in a bare majority report, but I think in this case there would have to be a very substantial majority in favour of the committee's report, and it should not require a unanimous report because we do not want a situation where one or perhaps two people veto the decision of a committee of this house. But if you had a committee set up with ground rules established, whereby there would

have to be substantial unanimity in the committee's report, then I do not think there would be any need to debate it at length afterward in the house. In that way we would either get a substantially unanimous report accepted with very little discussion or we would not get a report at all, and in that event we would still be faced with the situation which exists now.
I apologize to the house, Mr. Speaker, for having taken up its time, but I have stated my own feelings on this matter and I am confident that men and women of good will, as the great majority of men and women in this house are, can work out this matter sitting down together and discussing it. I am confident we can arrive at a solution to this problem, which is probably the greatest emotional problem we have been confronted with, certainly since conscription and possibly since the beginning of confederation. This country in its first century has shown evidence of the development it can achieve, and I am certain its second century is going to show greater progress.
I am confident that by reason, by good will, co-operation and discussion we will be able to work out a solution to these problems which confront us, and that we can look forward to the second century of our confederation's history with even greater pride than that with which we look back on our first century.

Mr. Speaker, on rising at this time to speak on the subamendment-and I understand we are being held very closely to the terms of the subamendment-I would point out that I desire to comment in particular on the first paragraph of the subamendment-"Are you in favour of the red ensign"?
I want, in introducing my remarks, to state definitely that not only am I a Liberal, but I am a Liberal of the Liberals. I would say to you, sir, there has not been a national convention of the Liberal party in Canada nor an Ontario provincial Liberal convention, outside of the Hepburn years, at which I was not an authorized delegate and entitled to vote, since 1923.
A national flag is the visible evidence of a country's soul and the symbol of its pride, and without it a nation is a dead thing. We have a national flag. We have a distinctive national flag.
Hear, hear.

I am very happy to live under it, and I will do everything within my power
[Mr. Nowlan.1
to maintain it as the distinctive national flag of this nation. In 1919, as a boy of 17, I spent my summer vacation in the city of Ottawa and was here when the national Liberal convention was held at which Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King was selected as leader of the Liberal party. I acted as a scrutineer, at the age of 19, in the federal election of 1921, scrutineering for Eddie Lapierre who was the Liberal candidate in Nipissing when we won that riding from Charlie Harrison, who had been a Union government man and in 1921 ran as a straight Conservative. For 45 years I have taken part in provincial and federal elections as an active Liberal and have voted in many parts of Ontario as I moved from paper to paper during the course of my university years, before settling permanently in Toronto on Canada's major daily and outstanding weekly.
In the Canada Gazette in 1924 we find a certified copy of a minute of a meeting of the committee of the privy council, approved by His Excellency the Governor General on January 26 of that year. It reads:
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report, dated 23rd January, 1924, from Right Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King, prime minister and secretary of state for external affairs, submitting that he has recently had his attention drawn to the practice which prevails of flying the blue ensign with the Canadian arms in the fly over the office of the high commissioner for Canada in London.
The reason offered for this variation from the union jack, which is flown over all Canadian government buildings in Canada, is to be found in the need very generally felt by Canadians in London for a distinctive emblem which will afford a ready means of distinguishing the character of the buildings over which it floats, and the portion of the empire to which they belong.
The Prime Minister considers that this purpose would be served by the employment in this connection of the red ensign with the Canadian arms in the fly, which though originally authorized by the Admiralty to be flown over vessels of the Canadian mercantile marine, has come to serve a wider application, having been displayed in times past from the government buildings in Ottawa, and quite generally throughout the country, where it is still often spoken of as the 'Canadian flag', meaning thereby, the distinctive emblem of Canada.
In this minute the word "distinctive" is used twice and the word "distinguishing" once. I quote further from the minute:
The Prime Minister, therefore, recommends without contemplating any variation from the present practice regulating the flying of flags from the government buildings within the Dominion of Canada, and assuming that no local regulation would be violated thereby, that the requisite authority be given for displaying the red ensign with the Canadian arms in the fly, on suitable occasions from all buildings owned or occupied by

the Canadian government, and situated without Canada.
I point out that when the Canadian red ensign was designated as Canada's distinctive flag, every seat in the province of Quebec was held by a Liberal member, and W. L. Mackenzie King, with that backing behind him, and knowing the red ensign was acceptable as our national flag, took the action which resulted in this minute of a meeting of the privy council. It still holds.
However, in 1945, at a time when there was some uproar developing with regard to a national flag, there was a further order in council concerning the use of the Canadian red ensign. It is P.C. 5888, dated September 5, 1945. It reads as follows:
Whereas the Right Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King, the Prime Minister, reports that by order in council P.C. 134 of January 26, 1924, authority is given for displaying the red ensign with the shield of the coat of arms of Canada in the fly (commonly known as "the Canadian red ensign") on suitable occasions from all buildings owned or occupied by the Canadian government and situated without Canada:
That the Canadian red ensign was employed by Canadian forces during the present war: and
That, until such time as action is taken by parliament for the formal adoption of a national flag, it is desirable to authorize the flying of the Canadian red ensign on federal government buildings within as well as without Canada, and to remove any doubt as to the propriety of flying the Canadian red ensign wherever place or occasion may make it desirable to fly a distinctive Canadian flag-
The order in council continues:
His Excellency in council, on the same recommendation is further pleased to declare and doth declare that it shall be appropriate to fly the Canadian red ensign within and without Canada wherever place or occasion may make it desirable to fly a distinctive Canadian flag.
Mr. Speaker, the word "distinctive" appears four times in these orders in council, and the word "distinguishing" appears once.
As an active Liberal I attended the 1958 leadership convention of the Liberal party and I voted wholeheartedly for the leader we selected; I would vote for him again if another leadership convention were to be held tomorrow. But I want to give the house some facts and figures with regard to the claim that this party is committed to the realization of a new flag for Canada within two years of election.
As I say, I attended the 1958 convention, and I attended the national Liberal council meeting in 1960. Normally at those meetings I am placed as a member of the committee on health and welfare or the committee on labour, sometimes on both. I am interested

in these three fields of human endeavour and I always will be.
At these conventions they hold a plenary session, as they call it. That is a fine, big sounding word. A plenary session is held just before a rally breaks up. Some pleasant things are said, good wishes are exchanged and the delegates go home. Usually half of them have already gone home before the plenary session opens.
Well, at this particular plenary session I listened intently while the recommendations of the committees in which I was most interested were brought forward as suggestions from the resolutions committee. I happened to be sitting to the right of a Liberal member of the Senate. The chairman of the resolutions committee said the party was committed to a distinctive national flag. This was the first I had heard of such a proposal and, let me point out once more, I was an authorized delegate to the convention.
I turned to the senator who was next to me and said "What is this all about? A distinctive national flag? I must get up and ask about that." He put his hand on my shoulder and said "Hold your horses. There is an element in the party that wants a distinctive flag, a flag different from the one we have now. But in the orders in council the word 'distinctive' appears and reappears. We have a distinctive flag now." "Well," I said, "If that's the way it is, I will keep quiet." I did not know there was any motion going in with regard to a distinctive flag. It was voted on, together with the other recommendations, about 20 minutes before the rump convention ended.
Later I looked at the orders in council, having never looked at them before, and found, as I have reported to this house, four references to the word "distinctive" and one to the word "distinguishing".
I	am speaking today because I do not believe the great bulk of the Liberals across this nation of ours are committed to the doctrine of a new flag for Canada different from the red ensign. I have in my hand a press clipping from the Toronto Star of May 19, 1964, in which William MacEachern, one of our ablest writers and a senior man in the news room of the Star, reports on the introduction of the flag question into this parliament. The first paragraph reads:
Prime Minister Pearson today invited the opposition to throw his minority government out of office in a no-confidence vote Monday if it doesn't like the government's flag policy.

I have outlined to the house what happened when I attended this Liberal convention as a properly designated delegate, as I have attended so many Liberal party rallies and gatherings of one kind or another. I wish to draw attention at this point to a piece of campaign literature put out by the Liberal party. The heading is "Time for Action-Vote Liberal". This was circulated in my riding in March, 1963. The country voted in April, 1963. There are ten pages to this small leaflet, and every word in the report was written by the national Liberal federation or the Ontario Liberal federation, the address of which is 100 Adelaide street west, Toronto, Ontario. I paid for the printing of upwards of 25,000 copies by Spalding Printing Company, 16 Queen Elizabeth boulevard, Toronto. There is not a single reference in those ten pages to a flag. That piece of publicity was given to me and, as I say, circulated in my riding of York-Hum-ber.
I hold here in my hands two pieces of Liberal publicity, one addressed to my

second daughter, Miss Catharine Cowan, 55 Humberview road, Toronto, Ontario, who is now a graduate of Trinity College and who in June completed one year at the Sorbonne in Paris and has a certificate for French and historical studies from that body. The other is addressed to me at the same address. There are five pages of Liberal publicity in this literature which was mailed out to I do not know how many people, and never a mention is made of the flag question in any way, shape or form.
I have another piece of Liberal publicity in my hand entitled "The story of Liberalism in Canada". I do not see any date, but it must have been printed since 1958 because it carries two pictures of our present leader. In this piece of Liberal publicity I am proud to read this statement:
The achievements of Mackenzie King and his colleagues were best recorded by the man who succeeded him as prime minister, Louis St. Laurent, who said in 1948:
"In recent years Canada has achieved even more than national unity within her borders. We had the unity required to make a vital contribution to victory in war. We have worked hard for the restoration of peace in the world. We have maintained in our own country a level of employment and prosperity never before known. Most observers, I think, would say that ours is the happiest country in the world".
They are the words of Prime Minister Louis St. Laurent in 1948. He said that "in recent years Canada had achieved even more than national unity within her borders." If we have not unity now, whose fault is it? The Liberal party was in power from 1948 till 1957 and we are now back in power again. During the course of the recent election campaign a gentleman came to me and pointed out that a booklet had been issued entitled "The policies of the Liberal party; general election, 1963". At the bottom of page 5 of this booklet I find this statement:
Within two years of taking office, a new Liberal government will submit to parliament a design for a flag which cannot be mistaken for the emblem of any other country.
I read this statement in this printed booklet and I asked my friend, a Liberal, "How many copies of this booklet were printed?" About ten copies came to my Liberal committee rooms in Toronto and I never knew one speaker to refer to it. Printed on it is "National Liberal federation, 251 Cooper street, Ottawa," and it is printed by Gauvin Press, of Hull. It contains the policies of the Liberal party. Long

before the bottom of page 5 is reached we see these statements:
It means adequate pensions. It means better health care, available to all when needed... It means.. .improving democracy in our political institutions.

The first aim of Liberal policies is a Canadian identity that creates unity without uniformity...
The second aim of Liberal policies is to increase our national wealth...
But security, happiness, achievement are not possible for us alone. The fourth aim of Liberal policies is that a growing, progressing, Canada will have a constructive influence for peace and progress throughout the world.
As I say, this statement about the flag appeared on page 5, almost as an afterthought. I have given hon. members the history of it, and I am glad to draw the attention of this house to this point.
Since this flag debate commenced I have spent three different Saturdays in Toronto doing research. I spent one entire morning in the offices of the Toronto Globe and Mail, another in the offices of the Toronto Evening Telegram and the third in the offices of the Toronto Daily Star. I enlisted the services of a very dear friend of mine who served in the first world war and has been suffering from the effects of trench warfare for more than 40 years now. He is a gold medallist in the field of advertising, a man respected in all fields of publicity in Canada. I asked him to note for me all the advertisements which had appeared on behalf of the national Liberal federation in the city of Toronto during the election campaign in 1963, and I have a complete list. With this list in my possession I went to these three newspaper offices and read every one of those Liberal party advertisements which appeared in the three Toronto papers. I have to report to this house that not once was mention made of any change in the flag of this nation.
Same old gang.

The Toronto Globe and Mail for April 6 said of this meeting on April 5, "Crowd fills gardens and Massey hall. Giant Pearson meeting and the crowd that flocked to the biggest political rally in Canadian history .. .There was a military band to set

the buoyant mood of the evening". But no mention of a flag is made anywhere in that report of the meeting. I sat on the platform and heard every word uttered in Maple Leaf gardens, but not once was there any mention made of a change in our flag.

The report in the Telegram for April 6 in connection with this giant meeting held in Maple Leaf gardens and Massey hall quotes the Prime Minister as saying that it was "the largest and most significant meeting ever held in Canada". Why was no mention made of the flag at the largest and most significant meeting ever held in Canada? This is the type of report contained in the three Toronto papers to which I have referred, and I can tell this house that no mention was ever made of the flag question. We were told always to vote for a stable government, because there is no alternative to a stable government. We have not got a stable government now, and if there is no alternative

what have we got? That is the question I put to this house at this time.
I would point out there are many references today that "Only by adopting a new and distinctive flag are we going to restore unity to this country. Only by putting up another piece of bunting will we restore unity to this country."
I should like to quote from the front page of the Toronto Globe and Mail of August 6, as follows:
The time has come to reach a decision on the official Canadian flag in the Interests of national unity and to give Canadians a much-needed sense of pride and confidence in their country-
That is what Mr. Pearson said.
I should like to point out that I for one have a sense of pride and confidence in this country, as I believe millions and millions of other Canadians have pride and confidence. I have not seen anyone running around with head down, despondent over the fact that we now have the red ensign as the national flag, as it was okayed by the Mackenzie King government in 1924 and again in 1945.
I should like to impress upon you the claim that the Liberal party is supposed to have a mandate in respect of the flag question. We are told that the government of the day has a mandate. I went to the office of the chief electoral officer and spent some time there on two occasions, as well as some time in my office here in the House of Commons doing some research in respect of this so-called mandate. I should like to point out that I am now speaking as though Sherwood Rideout, the late member for Westmorland, were here. The 129 Liberal members in this house do not even have a majority vote in the 129 ridings they represent. If we total up the votes cast against the sitting Liberal members we find they exceed the number cast for the sitting Liberal members. We are told we have a mandate, but I do not see how we can have a mandate on the basis of a minority vote. In looking up the definition of "mandate", it is interesting to find that it means "a clear instruction, authorization or direction." That definition is taken from Webster's third new international dictionary in the parliamentary library. One could also refer to Murray's Encyclopaedic Dictionary, which gives the same definition, and to the 1902 Contemporary Review, December, page 809, which states:
No practical politician can desire to lay too much stress upon the mandate theory of a general election.

When there are a thousand questions of the day how does one claim to have a mandate on any particular one, particularly when the point at issue has not been mentioned during the course of the campaign?
I should like to refer to an address given yesterday afternoon on the C.B.C. radio hook-up. The program is known to many people in Canada as "Capital Report". Yesterday afternoon Mr. Donald McGillivray of the Southam newspaper service spoke from approximately 2.20 until approximately 2.30. He was speaking on the flag issue. I hope most members heard his address, although I do not suppose many did in view of the fact that members are only able to take vacations on week ends. During the course of Mr. McGillivray's remarks he said:
Mr. Diefenbaker hasn't got the full support of all members of his party on his flag stand. The Quebec members have been the most unhappy since most of them have little chance of winning on a red ensign platform.
He then went on to say:
The Conservatives.. .in their speeches in the Commons have pounded away at two things... And the second is that people believe that the replacement of the red ensign by a new flag is some kind of concession or appeasement to Quebec-
The second is harder to answer because the new flag is, in fact, related to the needs of Quebec. There would be no urgency about changing the flag now if it wasn't for what is happening in Quebec. The Conservatives disagree with him but Mr. Pearson obviously feels deeply that the union jack on the flag is such a standing affront to Quebec that it must be quickly removed if the country is to be kept together.
But this attempt to meet the grievance of one minority group-
I refer to Mr. McGillivray's report because it would be heard from one end of Canada to the other on the C.B.C. network.
I was not in the house on Friday last. I went to Toronto on Friday morning to be present at the opening of the Canadian national exhibition which, I may say, does not enjoy a $47 million subsidy from the federal government but operates on its own. There appeared a report in Saturday's Globe and Mail in respect of statements made in the House of Commons on Friday regarding a free vote.
I should like to make some reference to this free vote question. How can we have a free vote in this house when the resolution stands in the names of the Prime Minister of this country and the Minister of Justice? I suggest there could be no free vote under those circumstances. There are individuals in this parliament who hope to be appointed as senators, judges and perhaps to diplomatic

positions. I am not one of those individuals. I am not a lawyer and could not be a judge;
I am not a diplomat, so could not be part of the foreign service. I suggest there is no record in Canadian history of a free vote question being introduced in the House of Commons by a prime minister of any day. There have been many free votes, but I suggest it is impossible to have a free vote when the resolution stands in the names of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice. I maintain that in order to have a free vote the resolution should be introduced in the name of someone other than those gentlemen.
Mr. Speaker, if you intend to restrain me I should like to point out that I am dealing with the main resolution.
Without attempting to be too facetious I should like to point out that before we can vote on anything we have to clear up the subamendment. I hope you are going to propose something we can vote on.

I suggest that we vote in favour of the red ensign when dealing with the first clause of the subamendment which reads:
That the amendment he amended by adding thereto the words:
"and that in such a plebiscite among the questions to be placed before the people should be the following:
1. Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign?
I ask the voters of Canada to vote yes in answer to that question when the plebiscite is placed before them.
Mr. Speaker, I have so many notes here I will be able to speak for 40 minutes on each and every amendment and subamendment that is proposed. I should like to quote from the front page of the Ottawa Citizen of Wednesday, March 13, 1963. The article to which I have reference gave me great encouragement during the last campaign, and gives me a good deal of encouragement now. In the lower right hand corner there is a two-column heading "Pearson doesn't reject red ensign as our flag". I should like to read this report, by Southam news services, under that heading:
Pearson doesn't reject red ensign as our flag.
Sherbrooke-Liberal leader Pearson said today he had "never rejected the red ensign as Canada's flag and do not do so now."
Commenting on reports out of Winnipeg last week that he wanted to see something other than the red ensign as Canada's national flag Mr. Pearson said that he merely wanted a distinctive Canadian flag.
This was Liberal party policy and in mentioning it to a group of ethnic editors in Winnipeg he said that "there are people in Canada who think
Canadian Flag
the red ensign can be mistaken for another emblem", such as the naval ensign or the Australian flag.
To reject the red ensign would mean the rejection of a British symbol, the union jack, which means much to so many people who have served and fought under it, and this he did not advocate. But he did want a search to be made immediately for a unique Canadian flag.
That quotation is from the Ottawa Citizen of March 13, 1963, within four weeks of the election in 1963 when this minority government was placed in office. I should also like to refer to a dispatch which appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail on May 16, 1962, written by Thomas Sloan who was reviewing meetings that took place at Chicoutimi. We have this report of a Chicoutimi meeting:
The fact, however, that the flag Is still an issue and not merely a means of getting applause was forcibly brought home to Mr. Pearson at his final meeting of the Quebec trip Monday night. There the Liberal member in the last House of Commons for the riding of Lapointe, Augustin Brassard, publicly pledged that if a Liberal government did not adopt a national flag in two years, "I invite you to ask me to return to private life."
Of course the next month Mr. Brassard was invited to return to private life.
He received hearty applause for that statement, as he did for another, which was perhaps a little more embarrassing for the Liberal party: "All across this country, Mr. Pearson has promised a distinctive national flag, without a union jack." The Liberal chief backed quickly away from that issue, contenting himself with saying in his address that he favoured "a distinctive flag for Canada which could not be confused with that of any other country." Further than that Mr. Pearson would not go, and he refused to make any comment at all on Mr. Brassard's statement after the meeting.
In referring to these statements with regard to the red ensign, I have shown you that it was not discussed at all in vast sections of the country. I make the statement to the house that this country has not given a mandate to anybody to alter the red ensign, our beloved symbol of loyalty and faith in the future. The Globe and Mail of last Saturday reports the hon. member for Villeneuve in this way:
Mr. Caouette regretted that statements had been made mostly by representatives of the Canadian west, that the proposed flag was nothing more than an attempt to please Quebec.
Of course the hon. member for Villeneuve does not know much about Ontario. He has not got a member from that area. No doubt he paid attention to the loyal speakers from the Canadian west, but I can assure him that on this score the feeling is just as strong in the province of Ontario as it is in the

Canadian Flag
Canadian west. He is reported as having also said:
We want Canadian symbols on our national emblem-not the symbols of France or the symbols of England.
What a sacrifice he would be making. The union jack is there, if he wishes to call it a symbol of England. Any symbol of France is not as prominent as the English symbol, as he prefers to call it, but he is willing to make the great sacrifice of ditching two things in order to get rid of one.
I would point out that when we are asked to vote on two flags we have this statement to bear in mind which was made by the Prime Minister on May 26, 1964 appearing in Hansard at page 3581, to a question by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Mont-calm (Mr. Pigeon):
Mr. Speaker, there can be only one national flag-
We who like the red ensign and who are willing to scrap for the red ensign agree that there can be only one national flag. A second flag simply muddies the water. My time is running short, but I hope to be able to speak again on this matter when the subamendment has been disposed of. On May 19 the Globe and Mail made this comment with regard to the action of the Prime Minister:
He has chosen to press the divisive issue of a national flag at a time when emotions are already deeply stirred by the question of national unity-or rather, by the lack of unity. ...It will be a long job, and in the course of it, Mr. Pearson may well find himself persuaded by the people that he made the wrong choice at the wrong time.
I am a convinced Liberal, a man who has always worked for the Liberal party except that I would not vote for Hepburn Liberalism in the provincial field. That is one time I voted Conservative; I voted for Dr. Minerva Reid. She was a prohibitionist Conservative, and they are very few and far between. I voted for Dr. Minerva Reid in Toronto High Park and I make no apologies for having supported her, even though she did not win the election. I say to the house as a convinced Liberal that the red ensign is Canada's national flag, that it should remain as Canada's national flag, and that if any changes are made in it it will lead to a division such as this country has never seen.
The Liberal government won a Pyrrhic victory in 1956 in the pipe line debate. We have not secured an over-all majority in the country since in four successive general elections. The problem is, who won what victory in 1956? Are we going to be like the Bourbons who "never remember and never

forget?" Are we going to try to force this divisive issue at this time and have to watch four general elections or more go by without an over-all majority for the Liberal party?
I would ask all members of the house to support the red ensign, which is Canada's national emblem and is known as such from coast to coast. We have not got here in this country a roofless ruin. We are a nation that was built with the support of Great Britain and the support of France.
Some speakers talk about now being the time to cut the umbilical cord that they say is tying us to Great Britain, but even if they cut the umbilical cord they will still want British investment. Canada is the biggest field for British investment. All they want to do is change the family name. I am proud of the family and nation into which I was born. I want to see the jack continue on the red ensign and I believe that to do otherwise will create a division in this country that generations yet unborn will be unable to heal.

Mr. Speaker, for several weeks now the house has been debating the flag issue, a debate which should have taken place more than 100 years ago when the Fathers of Confederation gathered to prepare, study and draw the confederation act, as they were anxious to build a great country which would become Canada, an international power. Indeed, by the active part played by its people in the making of a world still faced with the problems of peace, but a world which will finally find the peace promised to men of good will by the Infant in the manger.
In the darkest times in its history, Canada found amidst its people the strength, energy, courage, and generous men who did everything in order to save the Canadian democracy.
Since the beginning of the twentieth century, two terrible conflicts threatened with complete destruction the whole world as well as democracy, pre-eminent source of freedom; political, religious, social and individual freedom, freedom of the press, of speech, of action.
In those stormy periods, many Canadians, both French and English speaking, took refuge under the same flag, the flag of freedom, and there are many who sleep in a soil they loved to the point of martyrdom, smiling in their supreme sacrifice and repeating these words: "We die, but freedom and democracy do not".
I want to pay tribute to all those who gave their lives for the triumph of freedom and

democracy. I salute with respect those many veterans; we have the honour of having in this house a few of them who bear the scars of their courage and heroism.
Those veterans looked up to the red ensign to find the courage necessary to face the enemy. In the thick of the battle, when enemy bullets were whizzing on all sides and their comrades in arms were falling like ripe fruits, those valiant soldiers looked up to that flag which inspired them to charge the enemy with even greater courage and determination. They fought blindly for us, our children, our political institutions, our freedom and the survival of democracy.
Who could blame those veterans for being attached to the red ensign which for them is the very symbol of their present existence? Veterans, I respect you, I admire your courage and I understand you. You have the right to protest because some people would take away from you the red ensign you have coloured with your own blood and which, unfortunately, was too often used to bury a comrade in arms who had gallantly died on the battlefield.
My English speaking compatriots rightly love this flag which reminds them of their mother country. For them, the red ensign symbolizes the history of England, the triumph of the strong over the weak; it represents British institutions and the extension into the North American continent of the English civilization and the British culture which largely contributed to the greatness and prosperity of Canada.
For a great many new Canadians the red ensign means freedom; it is the flag under which they were welcomed in Canada, land of hospitality. They are rightly attached to the flag which meant the promised land of hope and, in some cases, deliverance.
That English flag, the French Canadians cherished it, too. Who, if not the French Canadians, made it possible for England to keep Canada in 1813, at the time of the American aggression? My compatriots cherished this red ensign at the battles of Verdun and Vimy, and just a few weeks ago we were proud to celebrate the twentieth anniversary of the landing in France, and the road to victory was paved by a French-Cana-dian unit, the Chaudiere regiment.
As a citizen from the province of Quebec I could remain indifferent to this matter of a national flag inasmuch as, since 1948, Quebec has had its own flag which the then premier of the province, Hon. Maurice Duplessis, took from the Cremazie monument, in the
Canadian Flag
Canadian metropolis, where it stood motionless. He gave it a new historical meaning and raised it on the Quebec parliament building in February 1948. The fleur-de-lis banner, which the French had abandoned in the mud of the plains of Abraham battlefields, after having been defeated by Wolfe and his men, and which was hiding in its folds the shame of defeat, that banner flies proudly today in the province of Quebec, where everybody salutes it with respect, pride and dignity.
My French ancestors became attached to the fleur-de-lis flag which, for them, was the symbol of freedom as well as the expression of French culture and civilization, and when they abandoned that flag on the smoky battlefield of the plains of Abraham, the French were defeated but not vanquished.
The Roman Catholic clergy instilled into my French speaking compatriots respect for the strongest, love for the new Canadian country and courage in defeat. The French Canadians gathered around the parish church, and faithful to their mother tongue, their culture and their faith, they worked to rebuild the Canadian nation. The French and English cultures found today in Canada are the basis of the moral wealth which our country offers to the rest of the world.
For almost a century, English and French Canadians have lived together under the confederation pact, and they sometimes worked hard to build up this country; like our forefathers, we have laboured to attain national unity. This national unity is deeply rooted in the confederation pact itself, and when every Canadian citizen lives up to the letter and the spirit of the confederation pact, then Canada will know the true national unity which, as far back as 1864, was the proud and sincere hope of Macdonald and Cartier, as well as of all the fathers of the Canadian confederation.
This national unity is going through a real crisis today, because of the flag debate, which may have disastrous results, by arousing nine provinces against the province of Quebec. I protest against the allegations of my English speaking fellow members when they say that this idea of a distinctive flag is one more concession to the province of Quebec. French Canadians never wanted any special privilege. They merely claimed, as they still do today- though somewhat more noisily-recognition of their rights, and they do not want to be considered all the time the cause of everything that happens in this country.
Why try to create the impression in this house and throughout the country that the government, by introducing the flag resolution, only wanted to satisfy French Canadians.

Canadian Flag
Personally, I have never been as Canadian as I am today, but if this discussion on the flag goes on in the same vein, I shall understand even better why so many of my French speaking compatriots are Quebeckers rather than Canadians.
If I were convinced that the government, in introducing its proposal, wanted to curry favour with French Canadians, I would vote against the choice of a distinctive flag because I consider that national unity must be founded on understanding, co-operation, harmony, good will and justice.
In order to favour national unity, the government has no right to grant one or several privileges to a particular ethnic group, even if this group is French Canadian. The government has a duty to treat all citizens on an equal footing, by allowing each and every one to use its rights in order to make possible the complete development of the Canadian personality.
I protest against those who claim that the fleur-de-lis reminds French Canadians of the most sad and shameful pages in their history. I will be careful here not to accuse my English speaking compatriots who would perhaps be ashamed also if they looked back on the behaviour of their ancestors. I am not ashamed of my history, I respect it; I also respect the historic past of my English speaking compatriots, I am as proud to be a French Canadian as those who claim with equal emphasis that they are English Canadians. I do not disown the historic past of my ancestors and of all the builders of this country when I contemplate the advisability of giving Canada a distinctive flag. The past must be the source and the inspiration of the present courage to determine the well-being and the future life of Canadians.
The "Pearson flag" proposal may be questioned by many, but personally I congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) for having the courage to put this question before the house. However, I blame the right hon. Prime Minister for trying to make a political football out of this important matter of a distinctive flag.
Why did the Prime Minister introduce his resolution concerning the choice of a distinctive flag with so much clumsiness? Did the restricted group of newspapermen invited by the head of government and who were the first informed of the choice of the right hon. Prime Minister deserve his confidence to such a degree that he neglected to inform in the first place the hon. members of the exact significance of his flag proposal? Because of his behaviour, the Prime Minister prepared the

stalemate with which the House of Commons is now faced.
Last May the Prime Minister stated that during the discussion on the flag everyone would be allowed to vote freely regardless of the party line. Later the Prime Minister indicated that he would consider that matter as a vote of confidence in his government. Last Friday the Prime Minister reverted to his original statement to allow a free vote to his supporters on the flag question.
In my group we are free to vote for or against the choice of a distinctive flag. Although the Prime Minister wanted to consider that question of a distinctive flag as a vote of confidence in his government, I was going to vote for a distinctive flag. But I would not want in any way that my vote be interpreted, in due time, as an unqualified approval of the policies of the Prime Minister and of his government. For this reason, Mr. Speaker, putting all partisanship aside, I shall vote for a distinctive flag and in due course against the adoption of the union jack as a symbol of our allegiance to the commonwealth. In accepting the explanation given by the Prime Minister on the resolution concerning the union jack, I ask him whether he would not see fit to introduce a third resolution to indicate our allegiance to the great United Nations family and a fourth to proclaim our participation in NATO activities, etc.?
The house has under consideration an amendment submitted by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and a subamendment moved by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More).
