I wish to point out first of all that I respect the opinion any hon. member may have on the flag issue. Some are shocked because a distinctive flag is to be substituted for the red ensign. If they feel it is their bounden duty to fight to maintain the red ensign I say to them: follow the dictates of your conscience. Although I do not share their opinion on the matter, I appreciate their feeling and I will not accuse them of fanaticism or racism, unless proof to the contrary is produced. At first sight, the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Regina City seems to offer an interesting solution to put an end to what looks like a marathon debate on the choice of a distinctive flag.
What could be the result of a plebiscite in the form suggested by the hon. member for Regina City? In my opinion, a majority vote on this issue would be the surest way to proclaim the red ensign the most popular flag in Canada. Would that mean that the red

ensign would be the choice of the majority of the Canadian people? I suggest that it would not, Mr. Speaker. The rabid supporters of the red ensign would vote solidly in the affirmative on the first question asked: "Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign?" The vote of those who favour a distinctive flag would be divided according to the preference shown for one or the other of the three choices suggested under the subamendment of the hon. member for Regina City.
To really reflect the feeling of the people, question No. 1 on the plebiscite should be amended to read as follows: "Are you for or against the Canadian red ensign as the Canadian flag? If not, which flag do you prefer? Then, the choice should be made among the three other suggestions contained in the subamendment proposed by the hon. member for Regina City. In its present form, the subamendment is dangerous because, on the one hand, it tends to confirm a principle, that of partisanship in favour of the Canadian red ensign, whereas with the three other questions which would be included in a referendum, those in favour of a distinctive national flag would be divided into three categories and the total results of one or the other of the three other categories or selections could be taken into account to try and upset the results obtained from those who would support the Canadian red ensign.
There is also the danger that a plebiscite would separate the younger generation from that of forty years and over. The younger generation, both French and English-speaking, wants a distinctive flag at any cost. As far as national unity is concerned, there would then be a greater cleavage between French and English Canadians. Such a plebiscite would give rise to controversies with regard to race, language, history and religion. Is there a country in the world which was ever called upon to choose a national flag by means of a plebiscite?
I feel that this is the responsibility of members of parliament, who were elected in a democratic way to look after the interests of their constituents, to consider and solve problems, and to adopt or reject administrative matters brought before the house. If the Canadian people were to settle every contentious, serious and important matter by means of a plebiscite, what would be the use of having members of parliament?
Personally, I am not afraid to assume here in the House of Commons my responsibilities in that connection, and if my constituents feel that I was mistaken in taking the stand
Canadian Flag
I intend to take, they will be free to dispense with my services in due course.
Next October, we will celebrate the centennial of the Charlottetown conference, which laid the foundations of the Canadian confederation. Is it not time more than ever for Canada to have its own distinctive flag on the eve of these centennial celebrations?
When I talk of a distinctive flag, I do not necessarily mean the flag with the three maple leaves, but if it is the only distinctive flag proposed to us, I will vote for it. Occasions of discord, dispute, discussion and flagrant injustice are too numerous and too often undermine national unity, for me to support the idea of choosing a flag by means of a national plebiscite.
I have always faithfully voiced in this house the needs, aspirations and feelings of my constituents of Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere who wish, with a few exceptions, that Canada be granted a distinctive flag, without publicly discussing the matter as it would be done if a referendum were held because, in my opinion, this would be disastrous.
It is quite difficult to deal with details without stating my views on the main subject. Mr. Speaker, I am conscious of the bearing of the statement which I want to make on the amendment proposed by the Leader of the Opposition. I am perhaps risking my political career, but in politics and as a practising lawyer, I have never accepted any half-measure, any compromise with my conscience, and that is why I regret to disagree with my leader on the flag issue, and I must add that I will also vote against his amendment.
In taking such a stand, I am renewing my approval of the political platform of the Progressive Conservative party, which also advocated the choice of a distinctive Canadian flag. As early as 1958, I promised the men and women of my constituency that I would strive to give Canada a distinctive flag, and if such opportunity is afforded to me by the Liberal party, I will lay aside partisanship and honour my pledge to my electors; I shall then have the satisfaction which stems from the fulfilment of one's duty.
On January 23, 1961, the hon. member for St. Boniface, Mr. Laurier Regnier, submitted a resolution which was discussed by the House of Commons and which read as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of introducing a measure to provide for a referendum concerning the adoption of a Canadian flag.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate with mixed feelings, as many members of this house have done. First of all, I feel no apology is needed for the length of this debate. This is a subject with regard to which members quite rightly wish to clarify their positions.

Since it is a highly emotional subject it cannot be dealt with in a hurried way and no one should be expected to avoid expressing his or her deep personal convictions in relation to it. We have already seen various changes in opinion-changes in the tone and temperature of the debate as it has continued -and it would indeed be foolish of any government to expect so serious a matter as this to be dealt with in haste or in a peremptory fashion.
Certainly, we have all been able to profit from the eloquent speeches made thus far. I have in mind contributions such as have been made by former ministers-among them the former ministers of national defence, forestry, labour and finance. My hon. friend from Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), was the latest of these hon. gentlemen to speak and his contribution, like those of his colleagues before him, could not fail to be helpful. These are all serious, experienced men with deep-seated convictions. I know, of course, that there have been other contributions of a high calibre, many of which I have heard. They are too numerous to mention individually, but I must refer to one speech, that made by the former minister of agriculture, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton). He too remarked on the sincerity of many of the speeches made on the subject and drew attention to the dignity they had given to this debate. His own speech added to that dignity, supporting as it did the suggestion made by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) that a small committee of this house be set up in an attempt to find some way of ending the unfortunate predicament in which we now find ourselves.
I agree with a previous speaker who said it was the responsibility not only of the government but of every member of this house to try to find ways and means of dealing reasonably and wisely with this sensitive subject. I regret very much that this debate is taking place at all at the present time. It has been given priority over other matters which we should be discussing as soon as possible. Despite the well ordered, well worded and conscientious expressions of opinion we have heard, this is a subject on which feelings can easily be aroused; it is a subject upon which misinterpretation can easily be placed and with regard to which misunderstanding can easily arise. The unfortunate incident which occurred this afternoon while one of our members was addressing the house is striking evidence that we are discussing a dangerous and divisive theme.

The hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) was speaking honestly and from his heart when he said it makes him bleed, as a Canadian of other than French or English origin, to find the two founding races fighting between themselves and using this contentious subject for political and partisan reasons. I am one of a great many of English origin who feel the same way as the hon. member for Ontario does. And I am sure there are just as many Canadians of French origin who feel sadness and discouragement at the increasing tensions.
We have a serious responsibility here, Mr. Speaker. An elected group of people naturally have a responsibility to deal fairly with, and solve by discussion and debate, problems which less civilized groups formerly solved by force. But particularly in a federal government we meet here with the recognized responsibility of having to deal with an enormous variety in geography, with many races and religions. We must assume that more tolerance and understanding is demanded of us. We in a federal parliament, to paraphrase a great Britisher, "were not sent here to witness the breakup of a federation". This unfortunately is not an extremist fear as exemplified by the many violent comments and actions. We have the best opportunity of any Canadians to get to know other parts of Canada, to hear about them, to learn of their feelings and their problems. We should therefore be in the best position to give leadership in strengthening confederation.
One cannot help but arrive at a dismal frame of mind when one hears on every hand disrespect for and lack of faith in parliament. I believe the general attitude to parliament has never been at such a dangerously low ebb. We all know from the record of other countries what happens under such circumstances. Respect for law and order deteriorates. People refuse to listen to those who have responsible positions and turn to something new and different. We know that criticism is natural, indeed desirable, and should be constant. But cynicism is not desirable. I am seriously concerned that during this past year the general attitude to government seems to me to have grown steadily worse. We in this chamber seem to have done nothing but disappoint and worry and confuse other Canadians.
We find ourselves in this comfortable chamber very much in the same position as students who have had the opportunity to be sent to a very expensive and very much admired boarding school in that, once here, we
Canadian Flag
spend our time debating the merits of our ancestry rather than getting down to work and studying the subjects which would be useful in solving the problems ahead of us. This is why I speak without any enthusiasm for this debate itself. This is not a subject which should have emergency priority; quite the reverse. While the country is divided on problems of health and welfare, on fiscal and monetary and tax problems which affect the daily life and well-being of each citizen, we are delaying facing this division. We are increasing it, because the longer it goes on the worse it gets and the greater is the need. We are daily opening new divisions and lessening the chances of unity.
The symbol of unity, Mr. Speaker, is not unity itself, any more than the skeleton of an elephant is strength. It needs the sinews on it and the blood in it to have any life or spirit. I think a Canadian flag is most important. I think it is so important that it cannot be forced. I think it is so important that it would be a tragedy if it became the symbol of disunity and, as has already been suggested, a political symbol.
Has there ever been a time before, Mr. Speaker, when we have heard such alarming and shocking talk-talk of one part of Canada separating from another? Have we ever before heard talk of the breakup of the commonwealth, talk of republicanism? This is indeed shocking, Mr. Speaker, in such a rich and young country as ours, which has had an excellent upbringing of law and order, where we should be full of enthusiasm, of optimism, of good will and good temper. I do not believe it is good enough to make political excuses. I do not agree that this is the fault of a minority government. Many countries have operated constantly and for many years with minority governments. A minority government does not need to be ineffective. Undoubtedly, Mr. Speaker, there are people in many parts of this vast and varied country who would like things to be different from what they are at the present time. With time, study and attention I would hope that many of their wishes and hopes will be fulfilled. But this is no reason at all to disrupt our national stability and make another group of people dissatisfied. What kind of future, Mr. Speaker, can we hope to face if we are going to follow a "rob Peter to pay Paul" technique?
The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) made a wise and mature sounding statement when he said, while speaking in this debate some weeks ago-I believe this closely resembles his words-that, "no one's tears

Canadian Flag
are to be ignored", the inference being that the striving people of one of our provinces, the sufferers from the yet unnamed and subtle revolution, should receive sympathy. I most heartily agree with this, but I am also much concerned with, and my sympathy equally goes out for, those who will suffer, and are suffering at the present time, from the ruthless and most unexpected discarding of things which they hold very dear.
If the hon. member for Leeds is right-and on this particular point I think he is right indeed-when he says that every tear is important, then I would suggest to him and his party that serious consideration be given to the tears of loss that many people will shed as a result of this proposal. It seems to me cruelest of all to toy with the intangibles of life. The hurts of extra taxation, the hurts of taking from people material things, can be repaired. They can be reasoned with; they can even be discontinued. But you cannot reason with someone who has lost a son or a father or a brother and who wants to keep what is to them-and no one can change it-the symbol of that sacrifice.
Canadians, Mr. Speaker, are very reasonable people. We are called reasonable people throughout the world. Canadians will compromise, will understand and will give in to a majority if they are sure it is a majority. But it is only fair to give them time to find this out. Pushing this debate, threatening no recess of parliament until it is through, gives an unpleasant impression of coercion which is neither useful nor sensible. If any unity can come, if any unity can be achieved by creating a distinctive flag, then by all means let us put our minds toward achieving it. But let us not merely replace one dissatisfied group of people with another equally dissatisfied group. Are all the facts of history going to be changed? Are we suddenly going to arrive at a new, mysterious understanding just because we fly a different flag which no one has ever seen before and which many people dislike? Far from it.
I am intrigued, Mr. Speaker, with the new horizons of understanding and the possibilities we now face for tolerance to and understanding of other countries and nations of the world. How are we Canadians going to achieve this understanding of other countries and other nations if we cannot reach some compromise between ourselves, and understand one another? How can we give the leadership to attain this goal of a modem world if we cannot get along together? I do not think

that the presently proposed flag is any contribution toward solving our problems in any way whatsoever. I regret to say that I find this whole debate ill-starred and ill-timed. It seems to me that we will not only end up with the cart before the horse, but we will end up with no horse at all. We are dealing with a catalyst, in itself a harmless bit of material, but once dropped into the chemicals smouldering in Canada, no one can possibly foresee the result. Mr. Speaker, such a gamble is not the course of wisdom, not even the course of common sense.

Mr. Speaker, in rising today to take part in this debate concerning the flag, a plebiscite and the particular design proposed, I find myself slightly confused. I prepared my speech some time ago. However, at the end of last week there was an obvious change in the attitudes of the leaders in this house, with some hope of co-operation. I may say this is a very welcome attitude.
A great deal has been said about this flag issue throughout the country, and particularly in this house. Many volumes of Hansard have been filled with speeches against and in favour of the proposed design. I should like to quote some of those words later on today. Many representatives of the people of Canada have risen in their seats in this chamber accepting the right, privilege and duty to express the feelings and views of their constituents. Many of these individuals have appeared as delegates rather than members.
As I have said, I was happy to witness the change of heart, if I may use those words, on the part of the leaders of the parties in this house, and particularly on the part of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). At an earlier date the suggestion was made that the vote on this issue would be a free vote. I think that suggestion was made even before the resolution was placed before us. After the resolution was made public we were informed quite clearly that the government would stand or fall on this issue. We were told we would have to accept the specific design proposed, whether we were in favour of it or not. Many viewpoints have been expressed by representatives of the people, and as time has passed there has been an obvious change. The Prime Minister I think finally began to realize that Canadian people were not willing to accept a specific design without having the opportunity of expressing their feelings. Many individuals have taken exception to the proposed design while others are prepared to accept it. Some people like the design, although I think they

represent a minority, particularly in my riding.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could point out the feeling in my riding by reading some of the vast number of letters that have been written by representatives of town councils in places such as Cardston, Lethbridge and Nobleford, as well as by secretaries of the various branches of the Canadian Legion. I could go into great detail to point out how strongly people feel about the red ensign. I must admit that there are some, particularly the younger people, who favour a flag with a maple leaf design, either that proposed by the resolution or one that has been suggested since, having only one maple leaf. The percentage of people in my riding who favour the design proposed by the Prime Minister is very small, approximately 8 per cent. The group which favoured a single maple leaf design amounted to approximately 16 per cent. The great majority favoured the retention of the red ensign. The great majority of the people in my riding are willing to co-operate, and will accept a distinctively Canadian flag other than the red ensign, although one having a similar design.
Mr. Speaker, very much has been said about this country being divided in two, one side in favour of the government proposed design and the other in favour of the retention of the red ensign. The meetings which took place last week apparently resulted in a willingness to co-operate. I am sure a solution to the obvious difficulty has not been found but I am very pleased to observe this willingness to co-operate.
Mr. Speaker, I must apologize for taking up the time of this house, but as I pointed out earlier, I feel it is my duty and privilege as a delegate of the people in my riding to bring their views to this house. It seems apparent at this stage that there will now be a free vote in this house, and I must point out, that being the case, that the people will not accept a distinctively Canadian flag adopted by this parliament without having the opportunity of publicly expressing their opinions. They wish to have some voice in the choice of a design, and I think that is their right, Mr. Speaker.
I did mention the free vote, Mr. Speaker, and I should like to say a few words about that subject. This means something to the Canadian people and to members of the house but, quite frankly, what it really means I am not too sure. I said earlier that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) indicated a long time ago there would be a free vote. Then he reversed his position and said the
Canadian Flag
government would stand or fall on this issue. Last Friday he said there would be a free vote. Members of the house know that a free vote means certain things. If you look back through history and examine the precedents you will find that a free vote really does not mean a vote on something brought forward by the Prime Minister of the country and seconded by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau). How can the house vote freely on a resolution brought forward in this manner? I sincerely hope this can be so. I am very optimistic about the trend that negotiations between the party leaders have taken and the trend that the debate in the house is taking, but I fail to see how we can really expect a free vote on a certain design at this late date.
I said earlier that there are people who are quite willing to have a distinctive flag. In fact, generally speaking I think all Canadians are quite willing to have a distinctive flag although their ideas as to the design may vary. As I came up to parliament hill this morning I noticed the flags of the commonwealth nations on display. There are many beautiful flags there and some I am quite sure we would like, but I was quite proud to notice the Canadian red ensign flying there. I thought it looked very beautiful and there are many people in Canada and many members of the house who think the same way.
I think the designs set forth in the subamendment are suitable for presentation to the public in a plebiscite so they may make their choice. As far as I am concerned, what I think I would probably do would be to take the red ensign and replace the union jack in the corner with the complete red ensign. There would then be a lot of room in the fly for green maple leaves, red maple leaves, a big golden maple leaf or a peace pipe as has been suggested by certain Indians. The views of the Indians have had very little representation in this house. I believe I have mentioned before that I represent the largest Indian reservation in Canada, the Blood reserve at Cardston, Alberta, and among my constituents is an Indian who is a member of the other place. These Indians have very strong views in this matter.
There are other Indians very close to Ottawa on the Six Nations reserve who pride themselves on having been allies of the Queen for many years. They consider themselves to be a nation and feel that they should be heard. They also pride themselves on the fact that many, many years ago they formed the first successful league of nations known

Canadian Flag
to the world, and I think they should be complimented for this. They have their ideas about designs for a flag if there is to be a new one and have suggested that a peace pipe might be included in the design; but not for one moment have they ever considered doing away with the union jack completely. In the opinion of many Canadians this is one symbol that must be included in any new design.
I have found that in the interval since the flag debate began up to the present time many people who were actually in favour of a new design, and particularly in favour of the one presented by the government, have been having second thoughts about the matter. I have realized from speaking to them that they have had little conception of what the union jack really meant, not only to the various provinces and areas of the country but to Canada as a whole. I could go into great detail in talking about the various crosses that make up the union jack, but I will content myself by pointing out that when you honestly and sincerely sit down with people and discuss this matter at length and in depth you find that many who had strong feelings earlier in favour of the new flag do not feel that way at this time, and quite rightly so. You talk to them about expressing the Christian idea in our flag and having a Christian emblem and many people ask what you mean. When you discuss this matter with people who do not understand and have not taken the trouble to find out, their reaction is one of amazement and they have very little criticism for the ensign. As a matter of fact, they wish they had not been so sure that they wanted to get rid of it.
I said earlier that much has been said in this debate. I should like to quote particularly a statement made by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) in concluding his speech. As found on page 6532 of Hansard, he said:
I say and repeat that we have everything to gain by remaining within confederation. We will be better oil financially, and the opposite is untrue.
That is what I want to say to the house. I commend the hon. member for bringing this point to the attention of the house. There are many others in the house who feel the same way, myself in particular. I am very glad that such a statement has been made because there has been so much talk about the differences between east and west and increasing the cleavage between the races. I deplore this kind of talk. Words such as I quoted from Hansard a moment ago are what we need in this debate and every other debate in the

house. It is this sort of co-operation which crosses party lines and races, Mr. Speaker, which will bring us forward not only to the designation of a distinctive flag but on so many other matters that face Canada today.
I wanted to point out as well, Mr. Speaker, along the same line, that there has been a great deal said about the cleavage between the races, the differences between east and west. It has been said that maple leaves do not grow west of the great lakes and that there should be all kinds of other symbols on our flag. I mentioned that in so far as the Indians are concerned we could have a peace pipe or a beaver. We could have many other things. Frankly, I like the maple leaf design very much, but not particularly the three leaf design. I believe it would be better to have a single leaf design. In spite of this adherence to the maple leaf I just cannot see throwing away the emblems of our heritage. In my opinion, we are just like a family. It does not hurt the younger members or any members of a family to have some sort of respect for their elders. Some people take exception to the fact that we want to keep our ties with certain countries. I know there can be a lot of arguments advanced and a lot of red herrings drawn across the path, but the fact we have the British North America Act which grants certain rights to people is a rather unique situation in this world today. It is something of which we ought to be very proud. If it had not been for the protection of the union jack I doubt very much if we would be in this house or have the British parliamentary system of which we are so proud. It must be a good one because it is about the oldest parliamentary system surviving in this world today.
Certainly, this constitution was given to us under the union jack and guaranteed to us by the union jack. It was given to us at a time when we certainly needed a guarantee. I just cannot see how the Canadian people can scrap this sort of thing and along with it the fleur-de-lis. When we talk about certain laws and principles, we must recognize our heritage from France. We have it in our language, not only in French Canada but in our English language. If you look for the definition of a word in the dictionary you often find that it is a derivative of a French word. I am speaking frankly and very honestly right now. It is difficult for me to understand French Canadians wanting to throw away the fleur-de-lis and the union jack, if for no other reason than their mother tongue

and the protection and guarantees which account for their very existence today.
I should like to say also, Mr. Speaker, that I am very optimistic at this point. I think that before long we will have co-operation which will not only bring an end to this debate but may even lead to some co-operation on the design of the flag. I have tried to point out time and time again that we are not adamant. I do not believe there is anyone in Canada who would not be willing to co-operate a little bit on a design for a distinctive flag provided, of course, that we keep certain emblems. We have noticed students travelling across the country, many being present here in Ottawa, and as a matter of fact in the galleries. I was back in my area, in the city of Lethbridge, for a couple of days. I was not on holidays, as I hoped to be, but I attended a civic reception. In that civic reception were 20 high school students from the city of Montreal who were visiting 20 different homes in the city of Lethbridge. As a matter of fact I sat beside the premier of Alberta, Premier Manning. I do not mean to give the impression that I am any more than personally friendly with Premier Manning, because he is of a different political stripe than I am.
I have always felt about Premier Manning in the same fashion as was indicated by the prime minister of Iceland. He was holidaying in Banff and I should like to quote from the Globe and Mail for August 12 a statement he made:
Prime Minister Bjami Benediktsson, of Iceland, holidaying here during a cross-Canada journey, says he is puzzled by the Alberta political situation.
"There's nobody against the government," he said. "It's rather an odd situation when you have a 63-seat government and only three opposition members-and so far I have discovered only one person who openly supports the Social Credit party."
I am only quoting this, Mr. Speaker, to point out that I am not that kind of politician. I do admire our premier, though, and I did attend this civic reception with him. These students were there. This was a good thing. The students were visiting 20 homes in the city of Lethbridge. I have not heard of another city in Canada that is carrying on this type of program. I am very proud of it. I mentioned something about co-operation, and here is a very good example of it. Upon further investigation I found that this was not an isolated instance, but an exchange of students took place every two weeks from the time school closed until it opened. The public school board and the separate school board of
Canadian Flag
Lethbridge co-operate in sending 20 students to Montreal and they are replaced by Montreal students who go to the homes these students have left. I am sure that this type of co-operation will bring about the understanding that Canadians need.
In spite of the extreme partisanship that my constituents have they are trying hard to understand other people's viewpoints, and not only are they trying but they are doing something about it in a very concrete manner. This is the way we will make progress on this matter. I would like to say I was never prejudiced, but there was a time during this debate when I almost was prejudiced. However, I am glad I was very patient and, as I said earlier, I feel much happier now.
Some 25 years ago I remember installing a heating system in my house. I ordered the apparatus from Montreal. It was a good deal, almost as good a deal as I could have had other places, and I felt as a true Canadian then, at a time when I had not the slightest idea I would ever be standing in this chamber talking about different flag designs, plebiscites and everything else. But I have always had that little feeling for my country and I am proud to stand here today and point out what my constituents think. It we talk a little more I think we will arrive at a distinctive flag that will make many Canadians happy and feel it is what it should be.
Surely the Prime Minister, the government and all hon. members opposite will listen to this sort of plea, and I put it in the form of a plea, that we do this thing. If we do we will not find complete agreement in every part of the house but we will have sufficient agreement so that we can go ahead and give the Canadian people a distinctive flag. Frankly, as I said earlier, I believe the people probably should have a choice, and various designs can easily be worked out when we come to that point. Some choices are indicated in the subamendment and others may be incorporated.
This is something I could not say several weeks ago because at that time this proposal was, to me, a political one. The three maple leaf design was definitely a political design and at that time I could not imagine its being associated with anything but a political flag because of the manner in which it was introduced. It was the design of one person, the leader of the Liberal party; but now I am happy to see the progress we have made.
Some people have been critics of this debate and have called it a filibuster, but if we in the great Conservative party had not taken this stand-and I do not agree it has been a

Canadian Flag
filibuster-we would not have reached our present point of progress. There is a much more happy atmosphere in spite of all the things that have been said, and if this party is to go down in history as being accused of a filibuster I emphasize once more I am glad to have taken part in it because, without it, we would not be at the point where we are today. I look forward to a time in the very near future when we will have a distinctive flag that will unite Canada and which will be of a design that is very acceptable to most Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be brief, but in view of the many letters I have received from my constituents I would be remiss in my duty if I did not make their views known to the House of Commons. I know other hon. members have received as many letters as I, and when they have spoken the papers have screamed "obstruction," "filibuster" and everything else. As a matter of fact one of the hon. members from Halifax used that term "filibuster" in his broadcast yesterday. But I point out that this is not a filibuster; it is merely bringing the views of our people before the House of Commons.
I have brought one letter along with me as a sample of the many I have received. It states:
Mr. Pearson, In his latest speech on the "Nation's Business," stressed two points: 1, the need for Canadian unity; 2, the need for a "distinctive" Canadian flag.
Regarding the first point, that is, the need for Canadian unity, everybody knows that the public controversy aroused to date by the introduction of Mr. Pearson's flag has reduced Canadian unity to the lowest ebb in our history.
Regarding the second point, that is, the need for a "distinctive" Canadian flag, only Mr. Pearson seems to be unaware of the fact that we have in the red ensign one of the most distinctive flags in the world. Where it flies on Canadian embassies, no one fails to recognize it as Canadian. Only Mr. Pearson seems to doubt this. Yet Mr. Pearson's flag-
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, is it not the custom that we do not refer to hon. members by their surnames but rather by the constituencies they represent?
I am reading a letter.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member, as I understand it, was referring to the text of a letter.

This is a letter I received and I have brought it before the house as a

sample of all the letters I have received. I shall continue:
Only Mr. Pearson seems to doubt this. Yet Mr. Pearson's flag possesses no distinctiveness whatsoever, and can in no way be compared with our nation's flag, the Canadian red ensign.
I think it is time, Mr. Speaker, that you know I stand for the red ensign and I am proud of it. Of all the samples and designs I have received at my office, the one suggested by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) is the most vacant looking. I think the right hon. gentleman is way off the beam in throwing away our red ensign, together with all our tradition, and proposing this new flag. I stand for a vote, and the sooner the vote can be brought about, the better. Let the people decide what they want. I do not believe that at any time in Canadian history one man has backed a certain design and forced it on the people of Canada. Therefore, I am in favour of the amendment and of the subamendment. I think we should hold a plebiscite and let the people of Canada express their views on this subject.
Just as an example of the publicity this flag is getting across Canada, and possibly to let us all have a little laugh, let me tell this little story. In our town, not too long ago, a man came out of a corner tavern, really loaded, and said in a drunken voice: "I am for a maple leaf flag. It has a bar at each end". That is an example of the publicity this flag is getting across Canada.
I know many who are present in this chamber will recollect the old song "We'll Never Let the Old Flag Fall". That promise is being broken by members on the government side-a promise which was sung with all our hearts in the first world war. No doubt most hon. members can recall, also, the poem by Dr. John McCrae, with its moving lines:
If ye break faith with us who die
We shall not sleep, though poppies grow
In Flanders fields.
Today in the House of Commons the government is breaking the pledges and the promises which were made in two world wars.
Our flag, with the union jack in the corner is a symbol that we belong to the great commonwealth of nations. I have been down in the United States on a few occasions in connection with defence installations, a joint effort by our two countries. On these visits I saw our red ensign flying side by side with the stars and stripes. I must say it did look

very good. It made me proud to have a part in that flag.
I know the maple leaf is Canada's emblem. But I should like to point out that the sugar maple is grown in only a small area of Canada, and that west of the great lakes we shall have to tell our children what those red blobs are on that flag-they have never seen a maple leaf. In fact very few maples are grown in western Ontario.
I am a westerner. I am a wheat farmer. Canadian hard red spring wheat is known all over the world and it is grown in every province in Canada. I think a sheaf of golden grain would be more appropriate as a Canadian symbol than a maple leaf.
How about a fish?

With these few remarks, let me indicate my intention to support the amendment. In my opinion the red ensign is more symbolic of Canada than any flag which has been shown to me so far. A Canadian can look with pride on this beautiful old flag and be proud that he has a part in it. I might go back a few years to the turn of the century when the western provinces were formed. People went there from every part of the world, from dozens of countries. We have a mixed population out there. And just ten years later they were called to fight for their country. We saw this mixed population take arms and go overseas to fight for the land of their adoption, with the red ensign flying before them.
It was only a generation later that their sons and daughters were called upon to cross the seas and fight for the land in which they were born. I say with great pride that the province of Saskatchewan, with its small population, contributed the largest number to the armed forces of any province of Canada on a per capita basis. This is something we are proud of.
I said my remarks would be brief, Mr. Speaker and I will conclude by saying once again that I will certainly support the subamendment before the house.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian parliament is now writing a very important page in its history. The debate on this resolution and its happy conclusion, with the adoption of a distinctive national flag, will stand as another milestone on the road leading to the independence of our country.
Canadian Flag
Following the Statute of Westminster and other important legislation passed since then, it will be a positive action taken by a truly responsible government and parliament and proof of our maturity.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is with a deep emotion and pride that I rise to express my humble opinion, as well as the views of my constituents, on the resolution under consideration, the purpose of which is to adopt a distinctive Canadian flag, as indicated in the resolution.
As could be expected, an amendment was tagged on without delay by the official opposition and it did not even wait for the house to vote before it moved an amendment to the amendment.
Having followed the debate from the beginning and especially last week, I will no doubt be allowed to say that I am completely against the idea of a plebiscite as suggested in the amendment of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), for two reasons.
First of all, if the national flag issue were dragged on the public and political hustings under the present circumstances where unfortunate statements and speeches are being made both here and outside, that would create disunity instead of strengthening national unity, which was the prime reason why the government introduced this resolution.
The second reason is that the Canadian people have elected in a democratic way representatives who received proper mandates to deal with the business of the nation. Consequently, the members of this house have the responsibility to execute the specific mandate entrusted to them. Settlement of this matter by a plebiscite cannot be seriously contemplated in a parliament where there is a responsible government.
The rare examples of such a measure in Canada repudiate any further application thereof, and especially in this case. Besides, we have the words of the leader of the official opposition himself to convince us of the inadvisability, uselessness and inefficiency of this procedure. Indeed, at time of the debate in this house in 1942 on the advisability of a plebiscite to relieve the government of previous commitments concerning the recruiting of soldiers for overseas, the present leader of the official opposition who was then member for Lake Centre stated, as recorded on page 186 of Hansafd for January 30, 1942:
Allow the members of parliament to vote on this question. Do not submit the question to the people of Canada, for in my opinion the taking of

Canadian Flag
a plebiscite at this time may well destroy the unity of Canada.
And the same person added later, when the decision was taken, as one can read on page 836 of Hansard for February 25, 1942:
A plebiscite is to be taken regardless of the fact that in the long history of Great Britain, with all the constitutional changes which have taken place, no government has ever submitted any matter to the people by way of plebiscite.
I could quote other testimonies as bitterly eloquent and perhaps even more so on the part of members of the Leader of the Opposition's Conservative family, but I am short of time. I will only remind the house, and more especially certain members opposite, of those words of the acting leader of the Conservative opposition of the time, Mr. Hanson, who stated during the same debate in 1942, as recorded on page 26 of Hansard of January 26:
Let this government rise to the level of its duty; let it not be afraid to lead. A plebiscite is not a policy; it is the negation, it is the avoidance of a policy. It is merely an unworthy expedient to avoid facing a vital issue. Its purpose is to avoid facing a vital issue. Its purpose is to avoid rather than to face responsibility; it is to avoid rather than to enforce the performance of a duty. It is not a declaration of faith; it is a declaration of impotence.
I know that those historic words have already been quoted in this debate; that is why I wish to do it myself in order to point out to the official opposition, and to its leader in particular, the strange, curious and contradictory position in which it now finds itself.
What more will the subamendment proposed by the hon. member for Regina City bring? Nothing more than the confusion which the latter has spread in the debate, turning it into an open, concerted and unfortunate attack against one of the founding groups of this country. That is obvious if you just refer to some of the speeches made in this house over the last week.
To those who, faced with their disappointments and their blunders, clamour in this house and elsewhere that the proposed flag with three maple leaves was designed to appease the province of Quebec, I will say that they are wrong to spread such untruths and to say such things because for a long time the people of Quebec have longed for unity within confederation. If for years they have been asking for a distinctive national flag, it is to strengthen that unity without which we cannot develop fully as an adult nation. That is why, although they are very proud of their origins, the people of Quebec want for Canada a truly distinctive flag which

will not bear any sign of subservience to either of its inhabitants' mother countries.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that in an adult country such as Canada, which is recognized as such throughout the world and by all international bodies, it is superfluous to discuss in 1964 the need for our country to have its own flag which will show in Canada and abroad that we are a sovereign state, an independent state, a symbol which will identify us everywhere and in all circumstances, as is the case for France, England, Ireland, Italy and all the countries of the world which can easily be identified by their distinctive flags.
Last week, I had the opportunity to meet delegates of the various commonwealth countries to the conference on education now being held within our walls. Without exception, all of them expressed the greatest surprise over those endless discussions concerning a distinctive flag and over the fact that our country is still without a truly distinctive flag. Among them was a representative of Ghana who could not believe that this whole debate was taking place. As hon. members know, Ghana is an African country and a member of the commonwealth which obtained its independence in 1957 and which has its own distinctive flag. Would Canada be lagging behind Africa? Unfortunately, we must admit that such is the case, at least in that respect.
Symbols play an important part in the life of a nation and the most important of those symbols, in my opinion, is the national flag. Now, a national flag must be distinctive, in this sense that it must not be confused with the flag of another country on account of any of its characteristics. That is why, with all due respect for the red ensign, which a 1945 order in council gave authorization to fly pending the adoption of a distinctive flag, we have to admit, with regret, that we never had and do not have yet a truly Canadian flag, symbolizing Canada as a whole and constituting the emblem of all Canadian citizens.
I think the time has come for Canada to have a flag which all Canadians, without exception, can contemplate with pride, a flag which could symbolize our great country, be the object of our affection and loyalty and become a rallying and unifying emblem, insuring for the future the greatness of Canada from coast to coast. In my opinion, such a symbol could not be put in better concrete form than is described in resolution 44A.

Indeed, are not the three red maple leaves on one stem the symbol which His Majesty George V attributed to us by royal proclamation on November 21, 1921? Before that, Queen Victoria had by proclamation dated May 26, 1868, conferred to the province of Ontario three green maple leaves on a golden ground which we find again on the escutcheon of the province of Quebec. The royal proclamation of 1921 which was issued at the request of Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, who was Conservative prime minister at the time, was the logical result of serious and deep-reaching studies and of the recommendations made by the special committee appointed after the first world war by Sir Robert Borden, another Conservative prime minister, to study the problem of Canada's symbols, which was considered of great importance. That committee, which, as far as I know, was composed exclusively of brilliant and prominent Conservatives like Major General Willoughby, G. Gwatkin; Thomas Mulvey, under secretary of state; Sir Joseph Pope, under secretary of state for Foreign Affairs; and Arthur G. Doughty, Dominion Archivist had considered the matter for several months. Whom of these hon. gentlemen does the right hon. Leader of the Opposition have in mind, when he accuses this government of breaking with the past; does he mean Mr. Meighen, Mr. Borden, Mr. Gwatkin or anybody else?
When suggesting to the Canadian parliament the adoption of symbols, and a distinctive Canadian flag, no hon. member in this house should try to express narrow nationalism. And the suggestion of a distinctive flag must not be interpreted in this way by anybody not sharing the views of those who favour this symbol of our maturity, that is, a distinctive Canadian flag.
It is not a question of denying our past, our history or our institutions. Quite the contrary, we must respect, and we do respect our past, our history and our institutions, and I believe that the adoption of a distinctive flag is the logical consequence for a nation which has reached nationhood; it is the greatest tribute we can pay to our past, to our history and to our ancestors who have built for us this great country of ours, so that we can, in 1964, live in a mature and sovereign country possessing the rights of a state which has reached its political majority.
To give our country a distinctive flag is to give the whole world, all international organizations to which we belong, all nations and all Canadian citizens in the first place, the 20220-455
Canadian Flag
proof that we are proud to be Canadians. Also, we are only attempting-and that is very important-to give to the spirit of our people, to the enthusiasm of our citizens, an emblem around which and under which our youth and the whole Canadian people can rally in adversity as in joy, in peace as during the dark days of war.
All Canadian citizens of any origin, of any language and of any creed, born on Canadian soil or who, voluntarily, sometime during their life, have adopted Canada as their new country, without repudiating their origins, have decided to leave the flag of their birth country and to rally under the banner of their adopted country to form with their new countrymen the great Canadian family which they and we want great, strong, independent and respected a mari usque ad mare.
Our forefathers worked too hard to pioneer and to develop this land, soaked with their sweat and fertilized with their blood, a land now the home of close to 20 million people, a country with all modern communication facilities, great natural resources, etc. etc., that this country should not have the right and the legitimate pride to display the distinctive signs of its majority.
To continue such wonderful work, I shall contribute to it with those of my colleagues who believe in the necessity for our country of having a distinctive flag, in voting with pride for resolution 44 (A) that is for the flag with the three leaves.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in this debate because, like so many other people in Canada, I feel very strongly about this whole issue. I should also like to mention the fact the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) acknowledged his feelings that hon. members would wish to present their opinions on this flag issue at the time it was being considered. I should like to emphasize that fact and deny the suggestion that we are partaking in a filibuster. I certainly do not admit that this is a filibuster and I will give more detailed reasons at a later time.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make one or two remarks about that what was said by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Bechard). He admitted that this was an important debate, and he is one of the few members on the government side who have participated in it. He said we were taking one more step towards independence. I suggest that is an expression of utter nonsense in view of the fact this country is completely

Canadian Flag
independent at this time. There is no subservience on the part of this country to any other country in the world. I should like to ask that hon. member what he means in this regard. Does he mean by any chance that this is a step towards the removal of our sovereign as Queen of Canada, so that Canada will subsequently become a republic? I should like him to answer that question.
With all due respect to the people of Canada I am sure they will laugh at the suggestion made by the hon. member for Bonaventure that Canada is at this stage something other than completely independent. This country of ours has been a country since 1867 and has, during these past years, become completely independent. I do not understand how the hon. member can compare this country to Ghana. I suggest the circumstances are entirely different.
Mr. Speaker, I intimated earlier that I am taking part in this debate because I feel very strongly about the flag issue. I should like to point out that resolution 44 (A) states:
That the government be authorized to take such steps.. .a flag embodying the emblem proclaimed by His Majesty King George V on November 21, 1921 -three maple leaves conjoined on one stem-in the colours red and white then designated for Canada, the red leaves occupying a field of white between vertical sections of blue on the edges of the flag; and on the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker, and on the amendment to the amendment of Mr. More.
Mr. Speaker, I have read the resolution in an attempt to point out that prior to June 15 the resolution up to the end of the word "flag" in the second last line formed part of a whole resolution worded in such a way that the red ensign was going to disappear entirely. Under the present alignment of two split resolutions it is still to disappear completely. Apparently to some this might appear desirable, Mr. Speaker, but I must insist that to millions of people across Canada it is next to sacrilege.
I have heard it said, as I mentioned earlier, that the red ensign denotes some sort of colonialism or subservience to Great Britain. Utter nonsense. I think it is well worth pointing out though, that while under these two resolutions the red ensign is to disappear completely from the picture as far as the people of Canada are concerned, the union jack is to be retained to be flown on certain occasions to denote our commonwealth relationships, or something of that nature. If one stops and examines the picture it would seem that for those who did have any idea there was any kind of subjugation or what have you by
[Mr. Monteith.j
Great Britain, the flying of the union jack under such circumstances would not be as acceptable as the red ensign. I know we are not discussing the second part of the split resolution but I do want to point out that the union jack is the flag of one country, Great Britain, and under those circumstances how can it be flown by us without denoting more subservience of some kind to that country?
I admit I have not made a study of the complete history of the Canadian red ensign. Others claim to have done so. I cannot cite certain dates on which it is presumed to have originated. All I know is that during the course of the debate it has been pointed out by many members on this side of the house that it has been flown as the flag of Canada for many years, certainly longer than I can remember. This whole question is not one of dates and figures. It is a question of the heart. It is the most emotional issue that could be brought before this house. I admit I am emotional about it but so are millions of other Canadians. That is why I insist that this whole flag question should not be before the house at this time. But, Mr. Speaker, as long as it is before us I for one propose to fight for our principles in this issue.
I know certain newspapers and other news media have taken it for granted that the result is a foregone conclusion. It has been said that no matter how wrong the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) may have been in bringing this issue before us at this time, no matter how many people may dislike the Prime Minister's personal choice of a flag, or how much, we should fold up and accept this dictum. No, Mr. Speaker, I cannot do that. I feel very strongly that in an issue such as this it is my duty to fight this coercion in every parliamentary way possible.
I do not accept defeat of the principles under which I grew up in this country. I do not accept the suggestion that having to fly this proposed flag is a foregone conclusion. I do not believe it is inevitable. It cannot be suggested for one minute that discussion of this issue is holding up the country's business. That is just not so. The Prime Minister has indicated that a recess can be had when this debate is over. We are not delaying the business of parliament. I admit we are delaying our own vacations but I for one am happy to forgo any vacation to prevent if I can this high handed, arbitrary action which would divide our country irretrievably for years to come.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) spoke the other day, and certainly

he showed a great deal more concern for the Conservative party than for his country. I suggest that he pay particular attention to his own party. No one has any mandate to bring in a distinctive national flag, particularly without the union jack on it at least in some form.
I was not present this afternoon for all of the speech of the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) but I am told that probably never before has a greater indictment been made of the government than was made by that hon. member. I feel that this whole question is one that should not be before us. I am repeating myself, but I feel so strongly about the matter that I say: If unity is wanted in this country, for goodness sake take the flag question out of parliament. May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

Mr. Speaker, before the dinner recess I had dealt with the fact that, in my opinion, the Prime Minister's choice of a flag is not inevitable, along with some other facets of the flag question. I had pointed out that 1 did not believe the question should be before parliament at all. I should like to mention one or two other thoughts I have had in connection with this matter.
I have had the honour and privilege of representing my constituency for something over 11 years. During that period of time I believe the citizens of Perth county have trusted my judgment on most matters that have come before parliament for consideration. I feel that they have sent me here to do my duty as I see fit. In all honesty, I feel that for certain matters, such as economic, fiscal and many other matters of this type that come before us, I am probably in a better position to pass judgment than a lot of the citizens of my constituency simply because I have ready access to the pertinent information. I feel it is my duty, after weighing all the considerations, to make up my own mind and act accordingly. To me, sir, this just makes good sense.
However, Mr. Speaker, on such a fundamental problem as the choice of a new flag, my opinion should not carry any more weight than that of any other citizen of my constituency. Their feelings on this divisive question are just as sincere as mine. I feel that certain 20220-455J
Canadian Flag
attitudes expressed to me, particularly by those who have served in Her Majesty's active forces, should carry as much or more weight than my own. The representations made to me, particularly by returned men but including many organizations and hundreds of individuals have, by a huge majority, been in favour of the retention of the Canadian red ensign. I admit that I have had some three or four letters indicating that the individuals concerned would be in favour of the Prime Minister's suggestion. I believe the huge majority, not only of my constituency but of all Canadians, would accept a modification of our present flag but certainly not the complete destruction of it.
I mentioned earlier that I had represented this constituency for some 11 years. Prior to that I had some municipal experience. I think that experience has led me to believe that on certain questions a plebiscite is a good thing. I was reminded just recently of an incident in my municipality which has had long range benefits to my city. Many years ago the Canadian Pacific Railway wished to bring a line into Stratford. Many business interests were in favour of this. They wished to have competition against the old Grand Trunk Railway which had given good service. The tragedy of the whole matter, Mr. Speaker, was that Canadian Pacific wished to have their roadbed come in along the river flowing through the middle of the city of Stratford. They wished to have their station in the middle of the downtown section, which is right in the heart of our parks system. This matter caused concern in the city. A plebiscite was held and those dreamers who could see the future of our parks system won out by a narrow margin.
I only mention this to show the benefits to be achieved by a plebiscite under certain conditions. I think anyone who has seen the Stratford Shakespearian festival would agree to two things. First, I do not believe there is any more beautiful parks system in any city in Canada, similar in size at least. I believe this was only possible because this plebiscite was defeated. Second, there would not have been a Stratford Shakespearian festival if we had not had this beautiful parks system to encourage those who dreamed. We all fully realize, I am sure, what that festival has meant to culture all across Canada. To me, Mr. Speaker, this is a concrete example of the long range benefits of a plebiscite.
The subamendment reads:
That the amendment be amended by adding thereto the words:

"and that in such a plebiscite among the questions to he placed before the people should be the following:
1.	Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign?
2.	Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign with changes made thereon to show the main heritages of both founding races?
3.	Are you in favour of the three maple leaves design?
4.	Are you in favour of a one maple leaf design?
This subamendment moved by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More) sets out four choices from which a flag for Canada may be selected. I have indicated, and I indicate again that my personal choice would be the retention of the red ensign, and there are many reasons for this which I will deal with in more detail later in my remarks.
This whole question is so personal and is of such a type that I do not feel the opinion of the most studied student of heraldry is worth more than mine or those of many, many millions across Canada. As a consequence, I feel these four choices should be at least presented to the electorate so that they would have an opportunity of showing a preference.
It should be noted that the subamendment states:
-and that in such a plebiscite among the questions to be placed before the people should be the following:
And it goes on to list the four choices. There are other choices which could be included if the subamendment carries, and such other choices might be decided by a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons. This has been dealt with in some detail by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) and several others during the course of this debate.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

No, not at the moment. You can make your own speech whenever you feel like it, and there are many other people on your side of the house I would like to hear speak also, like the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Harley), the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Beer), and the members from the Toronto and York ridings. I think they would be very interesting.
If the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) would only refer a study of this matter to such a committee it would provide a cooling off period, which I believe to be vital to the unity of Canada. Many hon. members in this debate have made just about the most impassioned speeches I have heard since I

entered the House of Commons. They were all from the heart. I ask the Prime Minister not to let them fall on deaf ears.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Speaker, I hear words of contempt, one might almost say of derision, from the other side of the house when I make these statements. I am serious. It is time some of you people got a little serious. I claim that this is no way to develop unity in the country.
Now I would like to say a few words on the various clauses of the subamendment and I shall first deal specifically with choice No. 3, the question dealing with the three maple leaves. I feel this is a reasonable choice to put before the people of Canada. The Prime Minister has indicated his adamant approach to this flag design. Indeed there has been a great campaign going on, and I am assuming this is backed by the Liberal party, to try by high pressure methods to sell this particular suggestion to the people of Canada. We have seen buttons, we have seen flags, we have seen miniature flags, and we hear of the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis) placing an order for 100,000 bumper stickers. If this is not a campaign I do not know what it could be called. Mr. Speaker, this commercialization of something which may never come about is to me deplorable.
I feel this is doing a great injustice to our present emblem, but despite the fact that there has been so much discontent shown in regard to this suggested design, I do believe that it should be included in a plebiscite from which a choice could be made.
I now mention clause No. 4 in the subamendment which deals with one large maple leaf in the middle of the flag, instead of three, and otherwise is practically similar in design to the three maple leaf design. I believe there are some who have indicated a desire for this particular pattern. Many representations have been made suggesting that even though preference might be for the red ensign, or a modification thereof, at least a one maple leaf flag would be better than a three maple leaf flag.
However, Mr. Speaker, I have to admit that the foregoing two suggestions-that is, the three maple leaves and the one maple leaf-do not move me in any way whatsoever. I fail to see how either of these two examples could be representative of all Canada. First, we know that there are many varieties of maple trees in Canada, and I would ask just which one is this? Also we

are aware, as the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Cooper) mentioned this afternoon, that maple trees are not a natural tree in the western provinces. Further we know the maple tree is much more prevalent in certain areas of the northeastern United States than in some areas of eastern Canada. To me it just does not have any heraldry or tradition behind it. Both designs leave me cold.
I now come back to the red ensign which is listed as No. 1 in the subamendment. It is not my intention to put a lot of quotations and detail on the record. I was, however, particularly moved and impressed by an article written by Mr. Stafford Johnston, the associate editor of the Stratford Beacon-Herald on May 26 last.
I do not intend to read the whole article but I would point out that it was written on May 26 last and shall give it in summary form. The writer started out by pointing out that 20 years ago that day he was in the line of vehicles, many miles long, heading for Portsmouth, about to go aboard ship for the landings in Normandy. That is in summary form. The author gives details of his experience during those days. This, for me, has great bearing on the feelings of many people across Canada, so I should like to read some of these details as given in the remainder.
The day we have been remembering lately was not D-day, but D-plus-5, when we came to the first moment at which I can remember any letdown.
On Sunday, June 11, 1944, our brigade headquarters was in the village of Le-Fresne Camilly. The invasion beaches were seven miles behind us, and the enemy three miles in front. The seven or eight vehicles that made up the headquarters were parked around three sides of a courtyard. The home of Mme Jeanne-Marie de Gastebled occupied the fourth side of the square. It was a big house, and it needed to be; one result of the invasion, inevitably had been the shooting-up, and bombing of a good many houses, and a lot of doubling-up of families in other houses. We never did get close to a count on the number of people then sheltered under Mme de Gastebled's roof, but when all the children came out in the morning to see the soldiers, the place looked like a schoolyard.
Some time during that day the Brigadier emerged from the truck which was his home and office, and took a look around. It was probably the first relaxed moment for him since the run-in to the beaches five days before. He noticed a flagpole in the middle of the courtyard and that gave him an idea. "Run up a Canadian flag," he said, in an off the cuff order.
This was, of course, a silly order. Modern armies don't carry flags into battle. During the weeks before the channel crossing we had all listed and checked, and counted and rechecked every item of equipment, and stowed and restowed it in the
Canadian Flag
vehicles, and the lists certainly did not include anything as unnecessary to battle as a flag. It was easy enough for the boss to toss off an order, but to us underlings it seemed obvious that the order could not be obeyed.
However, the signallers had an idea. They rummaged in a locker where they had signal flags stowed and, by a minor miracle, they found a Canadian flag mixed in with the kind of flag the signallers use for wigwagging. We found some rope, and somebody shinnied up the pole.
The French children watched all this, and some of them must have reported to their mothers and! their aunts. By the time the flag was ready to run up the pole, we had quite an audience of French civilians, women, children and old men. Madame herself emerged from the house, followed by a younger woman carrying an immense silver tray with glasses of wine. Madame made a short speech, and while we did not follow the words, we got the general idea that Canadians are a good thing. The brigadier, when he felt the atmosphere getting emotional, turned coward, and retreated to hiding. The rest of us tried to pretend we did not feel moved by seeing the flag go up.
It was the Canadian red ensign, of course.
The people, three miles away at the time, who might have wanted that flag to be pulled down, consisted of the two German divisions then opposed to 3rd Canadian division. The 21st Panzer division was a top rated division of the regular German army. The 12th S.S. division was one of the fanatical outfits in which every man was a nazi party member. For another month they fought us to a standstill, before we finally broke out of the bridgehead.
Hitler's elite troops couldn't make us pull it down, but now, 20 years after, it seems that a resolution of parliament may. Defeat comes strangely.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to repeat that last paragraph:
Hitler's elite troops couldn't make us pull it down, but now, 20 years after, it seems that a resolution of parliament may. Defeat comes strangely.
I should like to leave it-and I am serious about this-with you and the house for contemplation.
Now, we come to item two of the subamendment. It reads:
Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign with changes made thereon to show the main heritages of both founding races?
I, personally, could accept this suggestion. I feel the majority of Canadians would accept it and I honestly believe it would be the best compromise and the one most acceptable to our people. The fly might contain a large fleur-de-lis, or maple leaf, or the designer might put forward a design where both appeared. We could then leave the union jack in the corner. This would please all those who are in favour of retaining the red ensign while at the same time indicating to the rest of the world the value of the great contributions which have been made to Canada's history by those of French origin. We could be

Canadian Flag
proud of such a combination of symbols which would, at the same time, indicate the freedom under which we have always lived, and pay tribute to the heritage and tradition to which we have all grown accustomed and in which we believe.
On the evening of July 1 on parliament hill those present witnessed a sight which, I believe, will always live in the memory. At least, it will live in mine. It was a beautiful sight. There were some 66 red ensigns around the grounds whereas usually there are about 22. I admit the display caused me to become somewhat emotional, and I am not a bit ashamed of it. I was disturbed. I was frustrated. And I was angry at the people on the other side of this house who are trying to tear this flag down. It was a memorable setting, and to think there was any possibility of such a sight disappearing aroused strong feelings in many others beside myself.
I pass the garden of the provinces twice each day on the way to and from this building. I wish hon. members would go out there and take a look at the ten flags which are flying. There are three which have white backgrounds and insignia of some sort in the middle. I am sure all who saw them would have to agree that they cannot compare, in distinctiveness, with all the other flags flying there-the other seven flags. I do not say this with any disrespect for the three flags concerned and I certainly do not claim to have any aesthetic virtues. But I do claim that a flag with a white background is not good enough to be a flag of Canada.
I admit that certain people do not have the same feeling for the red ensign as I have. Some time in the future, when the present generation of older citizens has been replaced, it. may be that some change will be more readily acceptable. I repeat that nothing could be more divisive than bringing forward this flag issue at the present time. It is one which strikes at the very roots of all of us.
I remember when audiences in Canada did not stand up to a man for the singing of "O Canada".
Today this is generally accepted, and one would say that such hesitancy would be an irreverence and unheard of. Only time has accomplished this meeting of minds across Canada. The time may come, and conceivably before too long, when much more unity of purpose can be achieved in coming to a decision on a new flag or even a modification of our present one.
