Mr. Speaker, I do not think I started until at least five minutes after, but I should like to repeat one story to finish. While in discussion the other evening with the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) he mentioned a friend of his had been requested to ask the blessing at a banquet at which the hon. member was present. The words had impressed my colleague as they did me, and I trust he will not mind my passing those words on for the thoughtful consideration of the house. They were simply: "Oh Lord, help us to stand for something, so that we will not fall for everything".

Mr. Speaker, after having listened to so many excellent speeches on this topic I am afraid this one may bore you very much. However, as you have listened to so many I hope you can put up for a little while with some of the same ideas repeated in my own language. When one is making a speech, which must be about the one hundredth speech on this topic by now, surely no one would expect any very great originality or very much new material, and I claim neither for this one. However, since this is an emotional and historical topic and one on which one might be expected to have an opinion, as well as one on which one's constituents also have opinions which, as members, we ought to respect, I should like to state what are my own views and what I conceive are those of my constituents.
It is quite certain that the original reaction of my constituents to this proposal to change the red ensign to a new and distinctive design was one of amazed disbelief. This point has been emphasized over and over again. Is it true that the Liberal party did in fact pledge itself to introduce a new flag within two years of taking office? If it is, it has certainly never been brought to the attention of my constituents. Nor, as has been pointed out on many occasions, was it brought to the attention of the constituents in eastern Canada. This fact was emphasized very much this afternoon by the Liberal member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan), who stated that not a single advertisement placed by that party in the election of 1963 and published in Toronto had to do with a new flag. I doubt whether anyone in the west noticed that promise either. If they did I think they all thought this new and distinctive flag would merely be a new form of the red ensign. Or perhaps

they thought it might be a formal declaration that the ensign would be adopted.
After all, there is no reason why they should think otherwise. In 1946 the Liberals had been in almost universal approval of the red ensign. When the order in council at the end of the second world war during the term of office of Mr. Mackenzie King proclaimed the red ensign, that flag then began to have an even more general acceptance than it had had before. It was flown from public buildings, from schools under provincial jurisdiction in my own province, and largely substituted for the union jack which had generally been flown up to that time.
In these circumstances one can see why the Liberal promise had no impact. One can see why it was thought that the implementation of that promise was to be merely a confirmation of what was becoming an established practice. This view is again confirmed by the comments of the hon. member for York-Humber this afternoon, whose documented facts are well worth remembering. There was shocked disbelief on the part of the great number of my constituents when they realized that the interpretation by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) of a distinctive Canadian flag was one of a flag which had no element of familiarity or any historical significance. They reacted to this fact, as I said previously, with astonishment and then in many instances, I am sorry to say, with a great deal of anger. I received petitions containing literally hundreds of names requesting, and in some cases demanding, the retention of the red ensign. Demanding is a rather strong word in the English language, but it shows their belief that the red ensign has for many years been recognized as Canada's flag. Not one single letter of approval have I had from my constituents for the new maple leaf design.
Those of my constituents who are members of the Canadian Legion were among the strongest opponents of the new flag, which of course is quite understandable. Certainly they have a very strong belief that the red ensign is Canada's flag and that it was the flag under which they fought. No arguments from our Liberal friends can change that incontrovertible fact. I would not like to say that they fought for a flag, they fought for their country, our country. But to them that flag represented their country and they do not like to see it done away with and, rightly or wrongly, done away with at the whim of one man. He is unfortunately a man who has demonstrated that he is incapable of organizing the business of this parliament; a
Canadian Flag
man who does not have the genius for compromise which is so essential to the leader of a party. He is said to have had training as a diplomat. Heaven help us if our present diplomats are no more conciliatory or appreciative of the effects of stubborn, intractable action than is the Prime Minister, with his stubbornness on this flag question. I suspect that at 68 years of age he is in fact years older than the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) who chronologically is one year his senior. This could account for the odd things he does, like saying to his supporters that they could have a free vote and then emphasizing that his government would stand or fall on the result of that vote. Of course, he has now modified that stand. However, irrational attitudes are characteristic of the aged.
In putting forward the views of my constituents I would like to quote from a letter I received from a resident of Eston on May 21. He says, amongst other things:
Well, I am like a lot of the rest of the people of the west. I think the old flag should be left the way it has been for so long, as the Legion fought two world wars to protect it. So I hope the Conservative government-
-he was a little out there-
-will see that this is put to a vote of the people of Canada and find out for sure what flag they want. I don't like this thing of Mr. Pearson shoving or showing off. I think there is lots of other things Mr. Pearson could be doing besides worrying about a new flag. I have never heard of the U.S. wanting to change their flag and I don't think Canada should either.
This is the general attitude of the letters I have received. Rightly or wrongly, nearly all opponents of the new distinctive flag refer to it as the "Pearson flag". To illustrate this point I should like to quote from a telegram I received on June 16 from Tompkins:
Vote no on Pearson flag. Reasons, leaf design not distinctly maple. Jack absent.
I think these quotations emphasize very clearly what is the general attitude of my constituents. Those of the Legion who attended the recent national convention held in Winnipeg were incensed at the poor taste of the Prime Minister in making a controversial announcement to introduce a new flag at what they consider was a service of dedication and remembrance on a Sunday night. Why was not the announcement made at the opening session on Monday morning? This is the logical question they ask. And I ask the same question: Why had it to be done at that service, at what was a service of dedication? Did not the Prime Minister realize how controversial an announcement

Canadian Flag
he was making? Is this just another example of his poor judgment?
The legionnaires present on that Sunday night were indignant at the attitude of the press, who magnified a small disturbance into a major incident. Why did they do so? Was it to make the Prime Minister a martyr to those nasty legionnaires? While the legionnaires admit that some disturbance was created by a few, and I think under some provocation as a result of the Prime Minister's announcement, they consider that very little disturbance did occur. They cite the fact that the Prime Minister was able to deliver his whole speech as proof of the good manners of their members. When we remember the ill-mannered boorishness of an organized demonstration against the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) in Vancouver we can see that the legionnaires were well mannered by contrast and that the Prime Minister was bothered very little.
The Prime Minister has now precipitated into the political arena an issue which, in my humble view, time was solving for us. Very seriously his manner of attempting to substitute another flag for the one we recognized as ours was tactless and ill considered, and it was especially ill considered at a time when we have rumblings of separatism from Quebec. This is a time when the rest of Canada should not have its antagonisms aroused against Quebec, and yet this is just what this new flag is doing. Instead, we need a calm reappraisal of our attitudes and a sympathetic understanding of Quebec's problems. Surely the Prime Minister does not feel that his flag is going to contribute to such an understanding. It may please Quebec, but it will harden opposition to what may be Quebec's legitimate demands. From personal experience as the result of the few visits I have made home in the last four months I can confirm that this indeed is exactly what it is doing.
Whether he likes it or not there are many Canadians who think and say that this flag is just a sop to Quebec. I hasten to add, my party does not say this. I do not say this. I could not and would not, because if you will examine my name you will see that there is more than just a stirring of French ancestry in my past. It is true that may have been many hundreds of years ago, but I still have a very soft place in my heart for my French ancestry, and I resent any such thing being said. I would not accuse the Prime Minister of such political opportunism, but the accusation is being made by others. The Prime
[Mr. Cantelon.l
Minister could meet those charges with better grace if the flag had not been selected as it was selected by the cabinet and, hence, many people think by the Prime Minister himself. Indeed, the Prime Minister made it very plain that this flag was his personal choice. He alone then must accept the responsibility for the design and for the lack of judgment and foresight in introducing it now. There were many other ways in which a flag could have been selected and this suspicion avoided. Why was not an all party committee set up and either a single selection or a small variety of choices submitted to parliament. If this had been done parliament would have selected a useful compromise, no one could have called the flag a Pearson pennant, and it would not have been subjected to the ridicule which is now being applied.
I should like to quote from an article written by Eric Nicol which appeared in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of August 17, 1964. He stated:
Mr. Pearson's design for a new Canadian flag- the one with three maple leaves rampant on a field of whiter wash-has been greeted by a variety of noises, mostly rude.
That's the trouble with "making up" a flag. It's too arbitrary for most stomachs. We want a flag to have a background of tradition, history, battlefields and glory. The only way the P.M. is going to sell his flag is by leading a charge with it across parliament hill, inviting volleys of shot from a dug-in battery of Old Sweats, and going down with the bullet-shredded banner still in his hands.
Then, if he likes, he can call an election.
I do not intend to read the whole article but I should like to read one or two more excerpts. Mr. Nicol continues:
If Mr. Pearson is saying "Let's run it up the flag pole and see if anybody salutes," I think his design will run a poor second to the packaging of soapflakes.
The last paragraph concludes as follows:
Today when Canadian soldiers go into action it is under the flag of the UN, and a very fine flag that is, too. Why we need a third flag, except to shine the spotlight on at Maple Leaf Gardens, is not clear.
I fear that Mr. Pearson is going to be stung by his blue-tailed fly. And only one jack is apt to be jolly: J. Diefenbaker.
Now that the Prime Minister has forced us all into the unfortunate situation of accepting his personal flag or none at all, the hon. Leader of the Opposition proposes a way out. He proposes a referral to the people. It is a sensible way for an emotional issue like a flag to be decided. For this is purely an emotional issue, this has been emphasized over and over again, and one not to be decided

by reason except as applied to the emotional overtones of the issue. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) was, I think, the last hon. member to emphasize this very clearly.
One of the government members attacking the Leader of the Opposition's amendment said that it was just a smokescreen, that one could just as reasonably settle the pension problem by a referendum. This is a stupid comment. Is the member too obtuse to recognize the difference? The Canada pension plan is not an emotional issue based on the preconceived and basic stereotypes of a person. A member of parliament, or anyone else for that matter, should be able to debate unemotionally, and apply intelligent discussion to arrive at a reasonable solution of a monetary and social problem like a pension. He ought to have, if he studies the matter, a better informed vote on the pension issue than most of his constituents. But the flag issue is not in that class. No amount of study will make an M.P. better informed than his constituents on a matter that has its only foundation in emotion. Here, no reasonable explanation will sway many of the people. In fact, the only appeal to reason that can be made would be the one that, rather than cause trouble one ought to accept the new distinctive flag. Not a very cogent reason, but one which is sure to affect those who do not have very strong opinions, and I am afraid there are not too many of them. Perhaps the Prime Minister knows this and is acting accordingly. But if there was a referendum, no accusations that this was a politically chosen flag would have validity as they do today. Surely the Canadian people have the right to a flag free from political stain. The only way they are likely to get it is by a referendum or by a unanimous decision from a parliamentary committee dealing with the matter, which seems to me the most reasonable way to attack the problem.
Then too, the people have a right to a better selection than the one which is suggested. The proposed flag is a bad selection for it does not have artistic appeal nor as it flies does it have what I, for want of a better term, will call the clarity or stand-out quality in the air that one recognizes in the red ensign, the union jack, the French tricolour and the American stars and stripes. As one hon. member pointed out this afternoon, if you go over to the west block and look at the commonwealth flags flying there you will see that they have this quality too. They are clear-cut and stand out well in the air.
Canadian Flag
To illustrate further what I mean, some weeks ago when the new flag began to flutter from car aerials in this area one week end I sailed through the Thousand islands. There the Canadian boats all flew the red ensign and the United States boats the stars and stripes. Against the background of the shimmering water and the deep green of the shores these flags stood out clearly. They had clarity. As we returned to Ottawa we saw again the three maple leaves flag. It was colourless and insipid compared with those v/e had just observed. It does not have clarity in the air. Half a mile away it fades completely into the background. One might almost say it camouflages itself.
I wondered as I looked at it why the government did not select, if they had to have a flag of this type, the A. Y. Jackson flag. In that flag the blue bars were placed at the top and bottom of the flag instead of at the ends, and the red maple leaves were placed in the centre. Consequently this flag flies much better. It can be seen because it stands out against the sky without the white break in the middle which destroys the design we are asked to accept. It certainly is a much better looking flag, and this we might expect since it was prepared by one who is recognized as one of the foremost artists that the dominion of Canada has produced.
May I ask the hon. member if he would-
Later.
-vote in favour of the A. Y. Jackson recommendation?
Later, please.

speechtext: Order.

The flag is not an issue on which an election should be fought. To do so will arouse strong feelings between various regions of the country and create wounds which will be a long time healing.
Personally I much prefer the red ensign. We have had it as long as I can remember. It has grown to symbolize our traditions of fair play, our heritage of civil justice and our type of parliamentary government in which we all take our part. In Canada our flag has also meant freedom for many who have come to our shores from other countries with less happy governments. It has meant equality of opportunity for these people so that in the House of Commons the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp), the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Nasserden) and the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Kor-chinski) can sit on the Conservative benches
720S

Canadian Flag
along with a sixth generation Irish Canadian like myself and a Dutch Canadian like the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker).
The peculiar genius of the British parliamentary system has long been the capacity to compromise. Like many other systems have done, our parliamentary system would have perished long ago without that capacity. Indeed, it was because they knew of the justice and equality that existed under that system that so many immigrants have come to Canada in the last hundred years, and still come today.
Our French Canadian friends have been indebted to that capacity to compromise, allied with justice and fair dealing too, because their rights and their equality have always been recognized in our constitution and in our government. All we have to do is to look at our history, at the terms of the Act of Union, the Quebec Act and the act of confederation, to recognize that that capacity for equality and respect for others is demonstrated in this country today.
Only the strong, secure in their own strength, are willing to compromise. I would hope that the leaders of all the political parties have the strength and that the first element of that compromise can be set up in the acceptance by all parties of the suggestion to submit this whole question to a committee of the house. Without this first step there can be no compromise. I should like to refer to an editorial in the Ottawa Journal of August 19 which is headed, "Concession No Surrender" and reads as follows:
Politicians, the public, the press and the pundits of broadcasting hinder a solution of the flag issue by emphasis on "breakdowns" In negotiations, "escapes" for the leaders and the importance of "face saving". It is preposterous to argue that a concession is a surrender, or that to suggest an alternative is to be a quitter. The country is the loser if an impasse on the issue continues and divisions become so deep they cannot be bridged. The leaders, themselves largely responsible, should be thinking more of country than of party and those who encourage them in bitter conflict serve their country ill.
Without compromise the nation will be divided. I do not want to be a member of the parliament which does that. Under these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I intend to vote for the amendment and the subamendment. I cannot vote for the resolution as it is today. It must be modified. It must be submitted to a committee for a compromise that can receive the approval of this house.

Mr. Speaker, at this stage of the debate I do not wish to speak at any great length unless, of
[Mr. Cantelon.l
course, I get carried away. We have heard cries of "carried" from the other side on numerous occasions. I wonder if they are aware of what we are discussing here. I was of the opinion we were speaking on the subamendment and I am quite sure they do not want the subamendment carried. They must be thinking about the main motion.
Over and over again during the course of the debate we have heard that we were elected to take the burden of decision. I think the last person who said that was the leader of the Creditiste party. I accept that, Mr. Speaker, but I will not agree that we were elected to decide on a new flag in this manner. As members we were not even asked our opinion. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) brought forth a design with an accept it or else attitude. This we might accept in a dictatorship or a republic but certainly not in a democracy.
As far as the design is concerned, many people seem to forget one fact. We have a flag which many of us cherish, and along with most citizens of countries outside of Canada, we feel it is a truly distinctive flag. If we felt that we had no flag, then almost any design would be acceptable.
Dispense.
Carried.

Don't be in a hurry, you will get your chance. Surely the Prime Minister, with a better than average knowledge of psychology, could see that people will often accept gratefully something they have never had before, but will fight to the end to retain something they already cherish. To me, Mr. Speaker, the promise that the vote will now be free is commendable, but it has a bit of a hollow sound at this late date. We had this promise once before when it could have meant something, but it was withdrawn by the Prime Minister when he decided that course would help his cause. I believe I have said enough; I think you all have the message.
A referendum at this time would at least be one way of finding out how the people of Canada feel. It has been suggested that a committee might be another method. Why the insistence by the government that there must be a time limit on the debate on the findings of the committee? Certainly if the committee came up with a decision the members would accept it with very little debate. Perhaps I am of too suspicious a nature, Mr. Speaker, this attempt to limit free debate bothers me a bit; I do not like it. I should

like to make something clear right now: I do not look upon this proposed flag as a concession to the people of Quebec. I look upon it as a concession to the Prime Minister. Before coming to Ottawa in 1962 I had met very few Canadians from Quebec. Since then I have been impressed by their friendliness, their ingrained politeness and their moderation when controversial matters have arisen. Forgive me if I say there are one or two exceptions, perhaps. I would not presume to dictate to those Canadians what designs or emblems they should expect as a contribution to the make-up of our flag. I do reserve, however, the right to stress my own feelings in this regard and those of millions of other Canadians. We feel that those emblems which mean a great deal to us must be retained. This is why we are carrying on this debate. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, is that not reason enough?
I should like to read a paragraph from a letter I received. It is not from one of my constituents, but I think it covers a very important point and possibly shows the feelings of some people in Canada. I quote:
Friends and relatives who have been motoring from the eastern seaboard of the U.S. via Ontario and Manitoba told us last month that they had never seen so many red ensigns flying from every city, town, village, farm, barn and hamlet before. Other relatives who have just returned to Winnipeg from a motor trip to B.C. via Alberta, Saskatchewan, and of course, Manitoba, said that they had questioned many people on the way and where they stopped, and everyone was strongly in favour of the red ensign. All who did the questioning were young (thirtyish) university graduates with responsible positions and much common sense, so I feel their report carries some weight.
For those who would wipe the union jack or any other connection with Britain from our flag, I would say this-and I have no English or French blood in my veins but a mixture of three other races: To me, the union jack on our flag has no connection with imperialism, subjugation, slavery or any such thing. The very thought of this is ridiculous. It signifies only that our system of government is patterned after the British system which took possibly a thousand years to evolve. Our system of justice is also patterned after the British system. Is this not why millions of immigrants have come to Canada, because they realized they would receive the fair treatment here which that flag has come to symbolize? Otherwise, they could have gone to the south sea islands where, perhaps, the climate is better.
It is not possible for me to say how all my constituents feel on the flag issue. It is not 20220-456}
Canadian Flag
possible to talk to everyone in an area comprising many thousands of square miles, especially when we spend the recess in the House of Commons. Since the government has adopted the tactic of using controversial legislation as a club-they say, pass it or no recess -we are not likely to see much of our constituents. Unlike some of my colleagues, I am afraid I cannot say that every letter I have had has protested the maple leaf flag and favoured the red ensign. I can say truthfully that all but one have, and I have received well over 100 letters in that vein.
I feel that now I should read a few excerpts from these letters. I shall be brief and I have tried to choose those that deal with the amendment in question. This is the first one:
When I first went to school in Canada I was taught that the red ensign was the Canadian flag. It is one of the most beautiful flags in the world and has such a wonderful history behind it that I cannot understand the mentality of any true Canadian that wants to replace it. We do not need any other flag but it; it covers everything.
Please do everything to keep it. Nothing could replace it.
Here is another one:
I feel so strongly about the flag issue, I could scream.
Obviously, this one is from a lady.
It is only the thin edge of the wedge. If it passes, what next? The Queen? I feel Mr. Pearson is "playing politics" with the issue. I deplore such tactics. One does not just dump a flag and all it stands for-it is our very heritage. Fight for it.
This is the next letter I wish to quote:
Because I have very strong feelings regarding the flag issue I felt the best thing to do would be to express these ideas to you, as our member from Wetaskiwin. Please let us keep the flag we have grown to love and respect. Let us not just take a piece of cloth and put anything that may come to mind on it and fly it across our country and expect people to love and respect it.
We have grown up with our present flag. All the traditions and memories associated with this flag cannot be wiped out overnight and thrown aside. These memories and traditions that weave themselves into our country's life are very important to the morale and greatness of our country. If we must make it more distinctive, let us add to it, not take away.
This is a statement with which I agree.
The flag is for all our country, not parliament, so all the people should voice their feelings.
In other words, this lady is in agreement with having a plebiscite. I think that points out very well what some of my constituents feel. Here is a short excerpt from another letter:
It must be tiring to be battling away for ideals in the heat and humidity of an Ottawa summer, but it is proof that a large number of our M.P.'s

Canadian Flag
really and truly care for their lovely Canada and its future. Don't ever give up the fight.
It has been said, Mr. Speaker, that possibly the older people in Canada do not want to give up their flag but the young people are all for a change. During my last trip home I was interested in talking to a girl in grade five. She said that in her grade they had a vote on the flag question. In other words, a question was asked, do you favour maintaining the red ensign or do you favour the new maple leaf flag? This was the result of that vote, and it surprised even me. There were two who favoured the new flag and all the others in this school room were strongly in favour of retaining the red ensign. This gives you some idea of what some of the young people in my area feel.
I should like to make a short comment on the subamendment. In a spirit of compromise, we may have to modify the red ensign. If that is the case, it is covered by the second question. I believe this situation was explained very well by the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith). This afternoon, while listening to the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Be-chard) I heard him refer to the flags flying in front of the west block for the commonwealth conference on education. If I remember correctly he said that some of these delegates could not understand what the fight was all about. They had their distinctive flags and they could not see why we did not want one. In looking over those flags, I noticed that four of them, in addition to the flags of Britain and Canada, contained a union jack. I wonder what the peoples of those countries thought? Did they think that they did not have a distinctive flag? Did they also think they should get rid of the union jack?
If I remember correctly, he also mentioned that we should accept the symbols given to us by George V and Queen Victoria, in other words, the three maple leaves on one stem. It was my understanding that that was the reason for getting rid of the union jack and all other symbols-because they pertained to Britain; but here they are using this as an excuse and they want to adopt the symbols given to them by the British. I fail to follow this type of logic.
One of the reasons given for the choice of the maple leaves was that the army adopted them and used the insignia of the maple leaf. I, along with many thousands of Canadians, wore the fleur-de-lis proudly in my buttonhole for many years, as a boy scout. Is not this a possible reason for adopting the fleur-de-lis as a symbol. One argument seems as sensible as the other. If this gentleman is so

sure that all the ethnic groups want a new flag, and I think he said that, why is he so worried about a plebiscite? I think he is in for a surprise.
The three maple leaves are not too distinctive because I have seen many Esso flags flying over service stations, and under some weather conditions they are very similar. One constituent of mine suggested to me that we have a five cent stamp -with three maple leaves on it and now we are in danger of getting a five cent flag with the same three maple leaves on it.
Further, the one leaf design is not too distinctive either, and is not easily distinguishable from the Supertest pennant. In closing, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that both these companies have vast quantities of gasoline and therefore can afford to have a white flag and keep it well washed.

Mr. Speaker, I find it a little difficult to rise and speak on the flag issue after listening to so many eloquent speeches during the last few days, but I am taking this opportunity to speak as the representative of Assiniboia constituency because the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) extended an invitation to all members of parliament to speak on this matter.
At noon today I went outside my office in the west block and noticed all the commonwealth flags in front of the building, and I can truthfully say I believe any Canadian or any member of the House of Commons would be afraid to stand up and say that we do not have a beautiful flag in the red ensign. At the beginning of my speech I would like to repeat a few words which the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Enns) used in his opening remarks the other day, when he said that a nation should be proud to unfurl its new flag and this should be a time of excitement and enthusiasm. I feel if we were to have a new flag unfurled at present this would not be a time of rejoicing after all the controversy there has been over the present flag.
I have with me a copy of the Leader-Post of Wednesday, August 19, which had a report dealing with the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Sharp) and the headline says, "Sharp urges P.C.'s to end Filibuster." I do not consider that by taking part in this debate I am filibustering, because I feel that the Conservative party today stands alone in trying to save the Canadian red ensign as our national flag.
A short while ago the Prime Minister said there were six important items that had to

be attended to by parliament before a summer recess. If my memory serves me correctly, we are now on the sixth piece of legislation, and therefore members of parliament are dwelling on the flag issue on their own time in lieu of a recess. This brings to my mind a cartoon I saw not so long ago in the London Free Press where it showed a member of parliament with a shackle around his leg, tied up outside one of the windows of the parliament buildings, and the caption at the top read, "Hello Voter, Hello Nation, I'm in Camp Concentration." It showed all the tourists going by with those big carriers on top of their cars, with a little pup trailer behind, all going over the hill and out to the lakes, while we were sitting here. I feel we are doing this on behalf of the citizens of Canada who feel that we should retain the Canadian red ensign.
One of my reasons for taking part in this debate is because 1 believe a plebiscite is necessary on the flag issue. I am one of those who feel that whatever flag is Canada's we must all be proud of it and be proud to fly it, whether it be the Canadian red ensign as it is today, or another design which is the choice of the people; but like most Canadians I do not like to be handed an ultimatum, as we were in the case of the maple leaf flag. Under these circumstances I feel it is absolutely necessary to have a plebiscite in order that people all across Canada can have a voice in this matter, and in a democracy such as we have in Canada we realize that the people will accept the decision of a plebiscite.
I have also felt for a long time that the whole flag question could have been settled in a manner by which it would never have reached the point of disunity that exists at present. Had the Prime Minister called the parties together and said, "We want a modification of our new flag; you make the decision as to the type, but this must be settled," I feel it could have been settled by a certain amount of compromising in all parties. I realize that this may have been achieved, partly, in the last few days. The only regret I have is that the move toward agreement was so late in starting; too much feeling may have been engendered, one way or the other. If the present government continues to feel we must accept the proposed flag, then I think the adoption of the subamendment providing for a plebiscite is the only course I could support, providing, as it does, a way in which the citizens of Canada can express their wishes and offering the only means by
Canadian Flag
which they will accept a change of flags in our lifetime.
I should like to draw the attention of the house now to a series of quotations, all of which have a bearing on this issue. First, from an article which appeared in the Toronto Star on May 20, 1964:
As the drinks were served and the newspapermen nibbled on sandwiches, Mr. Pearson brought out several flag designs on cardboards, selected one with a cluster of three maple leaves and two blue bands and placed it on the mantlepiece as his choice. He said he was prepared to have the government stand or fall on the maple leaf flag. The Prime Minister was careful however to make it clear that the flag on the mantle was his personal choice.
Then, as recorded at page 3164 of Hansard of May 12, 1964, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) stated:
When the time comes to submit the decision of the government in this matter to the House of Commons, I would hope every member of the house would vote as his conscience dictates, and that there would be no question of confidence or non-confidence in a party sense.
The Toronto Star of May 20, 1964, also had this to say:
One week later he stated he was prepared to have the government stand or fall on the maple leaf flag.
Then, only last week, we heard it had been agreed that there is to be a free vote in this house on the flag issue. If there is to be a free vote, the best indication how members of parliament are thinking on this subject would be for all of them to get up and express their opinions regardless of which political party they support. In this way we would have an expression of the feelings of all members before the house. I believe the majority of the people of Canada would feel that some sort of justice had been extended to the minority, whichever it might be. All members would have been allowed an opportunity to express themselves in a democratic way. I realize that majorities have rights in our country, too.
This afternoon the hon. member for Gren-ville-Dundas (Mrs. Wadds) referring to the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) said there would be some tears shed on one side or the other. I think that is true. But I am completely confident that if this matter were placed in the hands of the people of Canada they would accept a decision reached as a result of a plebiscite. I see an hon. member on the other side shaking his head; presumably he does not agree with me. But I say the only reason the present government is

Canadian Flag
against the amendment supporting a plebiscite is that they know, themselves, that the majority of the people do not want the new flag design, and they fear the result of such a plebiscite.
I have had several discussions with hon. members on the other side of the house who have spoken in favour of a distinctive flag which has nothing to do with the past. I see one such hon. member present in the house this evening. I asked him: Are you not proud of your name? And he should be. I asked him: Are you not proud of your parents, your grandparents; do you not feel there is some tie between yourself and the past? I will not put on record the reply he gave me. But I feel very strongly that we do have ties with our families and our grandparents and we also have these same ties with Canada and our motherland, regardless of whether we come from England, Ireland, Scotland or France or wherever it might be. I do not think there is a person alive who does not feel some loyalty for his mother country.
I am one of those who are not ashamed of Canada's past in any way. Nor am I ashamed of the future. And I have every hope and confidence that Canada's future will be bright. I may add that I believe the sooner the people of Canada get back to having a majority government and two major political parties the better, for the biggest part of our problems will then be solved.
I should like to say a word or two about the word "distinctive". "Distinctive", properly used, means "distinguishing". As applied to the red ensign, it means that the latter is readily distinguished as Canada's flag. As no other country flies the red ensign, and as it has become known all over the world for over half a century, it is Canada's distinctive flag. The union jack on it signifies that we are part of the commonwealth-which we are indeed, in spite of the wishful thinking of some segments of people in Canada.
The true meaning of a free vote in parliament is one in which the members are free to vote as they wish, but in which the life of the government is not at stake. To say, as the Prime Minister does, that the coming vote is a free vote but that the life of the government is at stake is therefore a misuse of the word "free" as applied to a vote in parliament. Again, I realize the Prime Minister has now modified that position and has stated that we are to have a vote in the House of Commons which, even if the motion were defeated, would not mean the fall of the government.

I can truthfully say I would regret very much going to the people in a general election in Canada on an issue such as the flag issue.
I have here an article which I believe all members of parliament received. It is called "Remembrance Day" and I should like to quote three paragraphs. It begins:
Canada was not built in a straightforward, cut and dried manner, but rather has suffered cuts and bruises in its growing up. We are not a new country without a flag. Many countries have taken centuries to accomplish what we have done in 97 years-strangely enough much of it is under the ensign. During these years of growth Canada has always tried to make the world {as her men are serving today in many parts of the globe) a better place for all of us in which to live...
What surely could be more uniting than when persons who have worked side by side-Indians, French, English, Negro, ethnic and Jew, to build this great country in one century; who fought, shed their blood and immortalized the bloody beaches, trenches and battle fields of the world so that we might have what we now have- this opportunity of debate and personal incentive and independence. All this so that the ensign might continue to fly with pride over this land.
Certainly after having paid the greatest price- death-is this in itself not enough to make the ensign official. Or was this, the greatest of human sacrifices, meaningless and wasted. The least we can do now is show our humble gratitude, reverence and respect. Let us leave the ensign alone and make it official.
If we as members must decide, let us have a choice by getting together on three or four preferred designs with the understanding that we must come up with a flag of which we can all be proud, and settle this issue like grown up men and women in a free country.
I have here an article-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Have you anything else?

This article is from the Globe and Mail for August 12, 1964. I think this article is a comedy on the flag issue in Cyprus and it relates to the current issue in Canada. If I may I should like to quote part of this article. It is headed: "Canadians can't flee flag fuss", and is by Peter Buckley.
Any Canadian who hopes to escape the great flag controversy at home would be well advised to avoid Cyprus.
Flags in Cyprus approach the level of a national mania, second perhaps only to a day or two of shooting in the mountains.
In the Turkish sectors of the divided island, the question is straightforward. The only flag to be flown is the flag of Turkey-white crescent and star on a red background.
Well, almost straightforward. Since the flags sometimes fly for extended periods, the decisive red field tends to bleach in the sun to a pale pink.
Then it becomes difficult to tell the Turkish national flag from the flag of the red crescent society, the Moslem equivalent of the red cross, which flies a white flag with a red crescent over

its food dispensaries and other buildings in the Turkish sector. The weather tends to make that flag, too, look pinkish in time.
Then it goes on to speak about the Greek flag.
It is in the Greek Cypriot areas, however, that the confusion hits a fine peak.
There is the Greek-Greek flag, the Greek-Cypriot flag, and the flag of Cyprus.
The flag flown outside the Greek embassy here, for example, is a white cross on a blue field. In the centre of the cross is a gold crown. That, says the embassy, is the official flag of Greece.
If common sense were the sole guiding force, the official flag of Greece would be the most logical banner for Greek-Cypriots to wave in demonstration of their affection for mother Greece-the way the Turkish-Cypriots wave the flag of Turkey.
Instead, the Greek-Cypriots prefer the flag of the royal Greek navy. That flag is a series of blue and white stripes, with a blue and white cross in the corner-a design vaguely reminiscent of the stars and stripes.
For buildings of a public nature in Greek-controlled areas-historic monuments, police stations, government office buildings, and the occasional Greek Orthodox church-there is the genuine and official flag of Cyprus.
The situation being what it is, the official flag is among the rarest to be seen. Some Cypriots have been known to regard this as a blessing because the flag of Cyprus is the result of compromise.
The article continues but I should like to read only the last part.
Since the peaks so often look alike-and since the Greek and Turkish Cypriots themselves are scarcely distinguishable one from the other-a partisan climbing the hills for a day of rifle practice could become one of the rare battle casualties if there weren't a flag to guide him to the right camp.
The entire situation has been even further confused, of course, by the arrival of the United Nations.

In my opinion, he should keep to the resolution, as he is supposed to do under standing orders.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, this article says:
The UN banner-
Mr. Speaker, I ask for a ruling on the point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is asking for a ruling on the point he has raised. The only thing I can say is that I really do not think it is a point of order. I have been listening to the hon. member very closely and with interest, and it seems to me that this is part of his argument.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. In conclusion, this article says:
The arrival of a new flag to replace the red ensign over the Canadian camps, if it ever occurs, will only add a small ripple to the sea of confusion here.
I went home over the week end and one of my constituents asked me how we expect the people in Cyprus to be able to settle their issues when we as members of the House of Commons cannot settle the flag issue. She felt we were asking for a pretty big job to be done by our troops and the rest of the members of the United Nations force in Cyprus.
I feel in respect of this issue that members on all sides should have respect for the feelings of others, and that it will be necessary for all races and parties to realize that this may mean a compromise. I am sure that all hon. members of parliament can and will rise to the situation. I say that this is not a time to find fault without good reason. This is a time when serious men should reason together.
When I was travelling through Winnipeg recently I was discussing the flag issue with several people. One gentleman said to me that the only flags of the new type he had seen flying in Winnipeg were being flown on United States tourist cars travelling in Canada. Apparently the people of the United States have purchased a great many of these flags-made in Japan, I am informed. They think the proper thing to do when visiting Canada is to buy a new maple leaf flag and fly it during their visit to Canada.

Hear, hear.

Canadian Flag

I suggest to the hon. members down in the corner who are doing the clapping, that as a loyal Canadian, after we hold a plebiscite and find that the people of Canada favour the adoption of this new flag, I will honour it. I feel however that the people of Canada should make this decision.
Would the hon. member allow a question?

Mr. Speaker, I feel that I have only a few minutes of my time left and, as I said before, I should like to hear all hon. members speak on this flag issue and invite the hon. member to make his speech later on.
An editorial appearing in the Toronto Telegram on Saturday August 22, states:
The Canadian ensign must not be lowered without the consent of the people.
I believe that is good reasoning and the proper way to settle this issue.
I am not going to read the whole editorial, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to read two or three excerpts under the heading "Too Big For Compromise". The first excerpt reads:
It is far too important to be settled by parliamentary compromise...
It has been said that a plebiscite would be divisive. This is nonsense. Nothing could have been more divisive than the Prime Minister's introduction of the issue as a matter of high priority.
The article then continues:
Perhaps Mr. Pearson fears the outcome of such a testing of public opinion. Letters and petitions expressing determination to retain the ensign have been impressive.
There is no reason why this obstructive and divisive bill should not be shelved pending a reference to the people. There is no urgency. Most Canadians outside Quebec appear to be quite satisfied with the flag we have now. In Quebec the matter is of little importance as there they fly the Laurentian flag with its white cross and fleur-de-lis.
Until Mr. Pearson softens his stand, the opposition is justified in continuing a modified filibuster.
Again they have used the word "filibuster", with which I disagree. The article then continues:
As distasteful as such devices are in parliament, no other method seems practical in the face of Mr. Pearson's stubbornness.
The way out of the parliamentary impasse is clear: a plebiscite to end the long debate and to allow parliament to get on with more important legislation.
Mr. Speaker, an editorial appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail of June 2, 1964 under

the heading "Collision Course". I do not intend to read the whole editorial, but it does point out four errors the Prime Minister made. No. 1 was made when he promised a Winnipeg audience of foreign-language newspaper editors that a Liberal government would produce a distinctive Canadian flag within two years.
The second error was committed when the Prime Minister announced even before he had made a final decision on a design that he would take the House of Commons vote on his proposed flag as one of confidence.
His third error was committed when he told the Commons that it would have a full-scale debate on the flag, with this issue taking absolute precedence over everything else on the agenda.
Error number four occurred when the Prime Minister presented the Commons with a resolution endorsing not one Canadian flag but two. Mr. Speaker, I could go on and on but I feel there is little point in putting a good deal more on the record that has already been printed in Hansard.
Mr. Speaker, I have another article which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen on Thursday, June 18, 1964 under the by-line of John Walker, of the Southam news service. This article refers to the survival of the maple leaf. Mention is made in the article of the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson), and it states:
John Matheson.. .who advised Prime Minister Pearson on the adoption of the central three maple leaf symbol in the new flag, told the house Wednesday :
"Some people say this flag is a concession to the French Canadians. But they are part of us, part of Canada...
Every member of a family should be respected. The distress of one is the distress of all.
It is not a concession to do what is just and kind-''
Mr. Speaker, as we all know, and as has been pointed out many times, the maple tree actually grows in only about 5 or 6 per cent of the area of Canada. I would have no personal objection to the adoption of a flag embodying a maple leaf design as a compromise to the red ensign, if a parliamentary committee could come to a majority decision, or if it were clearly shown by a plebiscite that this was the choice of the people. I do feel with all sincerity and respect for hon. members from the province of Quebec, and others who feel we should get rid of the union jack on the red ensign, that that is not a majority view. I do not agree with that idea but feel that the union jack should be retained. I

know other hon. members feel the coat of arms, or the entire red ensign, should be replaced by a flag with a maple leaf design. We are grown-up men and women and should be able to sit down and settle this issue in a businesslike manner so that we can then carry on with important business of parliament. I am sure if we follow this course everyone will be satisfied, provided this is done in a democratic way.

Mr. Speaker, when it became apparent early in this session that the government intended to proceed with the introduction of a resolution that would lead to the identification of a flag as the distinctive flag of Canada, whether it was the Pearson flag or whether it was some other choice it was not unreasonable then for members of the house in every party to expect that the government, before introducing the resolution, would have first shown some indication that it was prepared to assess the feelings of members of the house and the people at large. But the government did not do this.
It has become apparent from what was said earlier today by a supporter of the government that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) consulted only a very few of his own colleagues and supporters. This of course is the very reason why we have been for some time, are now and probably will be for some time to come engaged in a debate on the resolution and the amendments thereto. For if it is our function here, as apparently the government expects it shall be, to designate a national symbol to represent Canada in the eyes of its own people and in the eyes of people throughout the world, and that we shall either confirm the symbol we have or find a new one, then it is only fair and equitable to every shade of opinion and to each member of the house that there should have first been a consultation and ascertainment of what would be both desirable and acceptable. But that has not been done and there is no sign it is going to be done.
What we in the Conservative party have been endeavouring to do and are endeavouring to do now is to provide the government and its supporters with an opportunity to reconsider their position, to consider whether they are following the best and wisest course, the unifying course for Canada in this issue. I do not think there is any doubt that the course the government has embarked upon has been entirely unwise and that it has failed in its purpose if that purpose was to provide a symbol with some element of national iden-
Canadian Flag
tity around which we could unite and which would draw us together.
I think the government has made a very great error in assuming that there was a tremendous desire for such an, extraordinary and total change in the flag of Canada. Perhaps it is true. Certainly there has been discussion for many years in many parts of Canada to the effect that we should in some way make the flag of Canada more distinctive from the point of view of our Canadian-ism, our history and traditions. I did not feel this was a necessary thing to do but I know there are Canadians who did, and who do.
If the government had decided that this feeling was really strong and if it had been prepared to respond to this feeling with some form of action that would have determined how deep rooted the feeling was, how great the desire was and what symbol of unity in the form of a flag would have proved most acceptable to the majority of people, then we should not have been able to fault the government for having moved in this direction. But we can and we do for the simple reason that if there was validity in what the government felt, it destroyed the validity of its position by the manner in which it acted because it did not ask the people of Canada to express their opinion before it brought a design for a flag into the house. It imposed a design, and not even a design of the whole of the party in power. It sought to impose on the house and on its own supporters a design of a small group. We do not know how many, but from what we heard from a government supporter today we are led to suspect that they must have represented a very small proportion of the total of government supporters. Instead of bringing before the house as a symbol of national unity a flag embodying the elements of unity, we have had thrust upon the house a symbol of division and we are still trying to live with it.
This criticism can fairly be made, and I only make it because I believe it is a justifiable and justified criticism. But there is a way out for the government. I think the Prime Minister recognized last Friday that his position was no longer acceptable and no longer in the interests of Canadian unity when he took the step of indicating that when the vote comes it will be a free vote. But what is the purpose of a free vote on a symbol that the people do not want? There is no purpose in it whatever.
I am not suggesting I can say to the house that the majority of the people do not want this symbol, but I suspect that is true. A great

Canadian Flag
many of my friends in the house also suspect it is true and I believe there are members on the government side who suspect it is true. Consequently, if there is this suspicion in the house now to any substantial extent, then steps must be taken to eliminate the possibility of a dreadful mistake if we impose this flag on Canada; because if we do, the emotions of the people of Canada and their relationships with one another will be torn asunder, particularly so far as the racial groupings in the nation are concerned. If it leads to a division, then any move to accept this flag is a fatal move in the life of Canada. If not fatal, the wound will run deep and blood will flow long and the nation will take a long time to recover its strength afterward. This must not happen.
There is no necessity for a flag to be imposed. If there is any danger that one is about to be imposed, we have a way out. We can simply provide the people with an opportunity to express their opinions about the ensign, the flag which has represented Canada and by which Canada has been known throughout most of its history, if not always in its present form then in evolution to the present form. As a native born Canadian whose ancestors have been here for several generations, although not for as many generations as the ancestors of others in the house, this flag is to me the flag of Canada, because of the place of my birth, the environment in which I grew up and the traditions to which I am unquestionably attached. There is no doubt in my mind about this. But I realize there are others who do not have this feeling as strongly as I do and if they are in the majority they should be provided with the opportunity to demonstrate that fact. If they are not in the majority, if the majority of Canadians still wish to retain the national flag under which they have lived their lives and served the nation in peace and in war, then they should be provided an opportunity to indicate that fact.
After all, there has been a great deal of talk, Mr. Speaker, about service on foreign battlefields under the red ensign. It is not just those who served Canada in the armed forces in world war I, world war II or any other international engagement in which this country has taken part, who have served Canada under that flag. Every soul who has lived his life in Canada, raised his family in Canada, served his country in any capacity, however great or small, has served it under that flag. His attachment to that symbol, to that flag, is equally strong. Therefore, sir, it should be discovered, first, how strongly this desire runs in the nation for a change and
[Mr. Fleming (Okanagan-Revelstoke) .1
whether, in fact, a change at this time would be or could be a unifying factor or whether it would be more likely a dividing factor. There is the justification for a plebiscite.
If the plebiscite is rejected-and there are those who feel it is a cumbersome method, would take too long or cost too much-then there is the parliamentary committee. A plebiscite could preserve the unity of the nation on this question. However, if a parliamentary committee were decided upon, the members of this house from all parties could gather in the less fervid atmosphere of a committee, away from the pressures of debate on this floor, away from the attentions of the press and public, to examine the possibilities of the various courses that could be followed. They could endeavour to discover what the people of Canada are thinking. If necessary, that committee could travel from coast to coast holding hearings and calling the people before them to give evidence. If this is necessary, then let us do that. Somehow or other, there must be consultation. There must be some more effective means found of ascertaining what this action we are expected to take will mean in terms of our national harmony, of our national existence.
It need not prove that I am right when I indicate my attachment to the ensign. It may not prove that the government is right. However, there may be some common ground between the two positions that would be acceptable to all Canadians. If the government persists in going ahead on the course it is following, it will never know until it is too late. After this house endorses this resolution establishing the proposed flag as the flag of Canada, then that is the end of the matter. This becomes the flag of Canada whether or not the people want it, whether they are prepared to live with it or not, whether it divides the nation or not. I do not believe it is up to us to take that gamble. This is no ordinary piece of legislation that we have been asked to pass. If there is a change of government there will be no opportunity to pass amending legislation in connection with the flag, as we would if this were an ordinary piece of legislation which a succeeding government might find unsatisfactory to it-unless, of course, we are going to adopt party flags, and have rotational flags that change every time the government changes. This would be about as ridiculous as the situation we are facing now, when we are presented with a flag design that does not meet with the wishes of the majority of

the people in their desire for a national symbol.
This debate has been going on for some time, and as I say it will likely go on a good deal longer unless the government recognizes that there is no necessity to thrust this proposed design down the throats of the members of this parliament. There is no necessity to take that gamble. There is not necessity to risk a mistake. The government can take action that will either confirm or deny the validity of its position. Equally, it could prove to the opposition whether or not it has been following a valid course in the eyes of the people. In my judgment, the course upon which we are now set leaves no alternative to us but to put forward every argument that we can, those of us who feel as I do, that this motion should not come to a vote; that this motion is a mistake and the ensign still represents the flag desired by the majority; that if a change were desirable, the majority would still prefer a flag which evolved from the ensign and which retained some of the elements of it. Since we feel this way, we cannot allow the government to secure the adoption of the resolution which may have far reaching and damaging effects on the structure and the harmony of the nation.
I come back to my original suggestion, sir. The thing that is so difficult to understand is that this issue, of all issues, should have given rise to so much antagonism and bitterness in this house, that there should be suggestions that those of us who have a certain affinity for the ensign are colonially minded or that the proponents of the three maple leaf design should eliminate all our Canadian heritage and tradition, and that this sort of thing should become the daily currency of discussion in this house and in the exchange of ideas between Canadians. It is a tragedy that this should have happened, because I am sure no member in this house who discussed this matter two years ago would have assumed that when this question came to the floor of this house for debate there would be anything but a substantial degree of unanimity amongst members, regardless of party. They would have assumed there would be no partisan division, no major fragmentation of the nation. There would be some basis worked out carefully, after consultation, and there would be common ground both in the house and in the nation.
This has not been done. This debate is evidence of that, and it would never have taken place if that had been done. This is the charge we are making against the government. No
Canadian Flag
effort was made to create an atmosphere, either in the house or in the country, conducive to the acceptance of this distinctive national flag which would, in fact, represent the Canadian nation to all its people and to all the people in the world wherever that flag was flown.
So, sir, I would ask the government and its supporters to realize that there is an opportunity to change the course of this divisive debate. There is a means by which unity can be found on this question, but it is now in the hands of the government members to decide, in consultation with their leaders and in particular with the Prime Minister, whether that course is to be followed or not.

Mr. Speaker, we are stalled on a flag debate of the government's choosing and, as the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Watson) pointed out, we are taking up our recess to defend the right of each Canadian to have some say in what flag he shall adopt as the symbol for his country.
From time to time we have asked the government to introduce legislation which its members cried for in 1963. They said at that time legislation was necessary arising out of the royal commissions on transportations and on magazines, and they forced an election because they thought this legislation was not coming forth. For the past two months we on this side have been asking them to bring on this legislation. We will deal with it and in due course pass it, as we have done already in some instances. But today we are bogged down on a resolution introduced by a very stubborn government which is bent on ramming the three maple leaf design down the throats of members of this house and of all Canadians.
The three maple leaf design is the design of the Prime Minister, and perhaps of the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson). I do not know just what part the latter played in it, although on this particular issue the newspapers give him credit for being the man behind the man. Now we hear some talk that there is to be a free vote and that the trained seals over there-
Oh, oh.

A noted writer who is also a member of this house does not like those words "trained seals". He is entitled to his opinion, but hon. members opposite have been very active in this debate by simply sitting in their seats and making a lot of noise when they thought it was appropriate. However, very few of them have

Canadian Flag
risen to defend their Prime Minister and to say why Canadians should accept his design.
The Prime Minister has said he will give them a free vote, but I do not quite see a bunch of swallows flying forth flapping their wings freely. As recorded in Hansard of May 12 the Prime Minister said that when the time came to submit the government's decision on this matter to the House of Commons he hoped every member of the house would vote as his conscience dictated, and that there would be no question of confidence or non-confidence in a party sense.
Later, on about May 20, he stated he was prepared to have his government stand or fall on the flag issue. He considered the problem in the interval and realized that he had better whip the boys into line. Maybe a few of them told him about their problems with their constituents, and from May 20, almost for three months, he has had them toeing the mark. Now he has turned them loose, hoping we would think they could go back to their original thoughts on the flag. They were sold a bill of goods on May 20. They accepted a bill of goods on May 20, and therefore the announcement of a free vote at this time means very little because they cannot go back on the words they have spoken to their constituents during the last few months.
We in the opposition have a duty to perform. At the very outset we realized a flag debate would be one in which very many people would have numerous ideas to put forward with regard to Canada's flag. Now we have heard from people all across Canada on the proposed design of the Prime Minister, and it was our duty to show the opposition that was evident in the country with regard to this design. We have done just that and we may continue to do just that.
We also hear some talk that the government is prepared to accept the one maple leaf design put forward by the New Democratic party, but we do not know whether this is a fact or not.
Would you accept it?

Many things enter into making a choice. It depends on what colour it is. There would be great similarity between one red maple leaf on a white background, and the red cross. I think it is our duty to know what the issues are. This business of picking up by way of the grapevine that the government is prepared to accept one maple leaf is not good enough. We are all grown men and women and should be able to realize that the opposition in the

country to the three maple leaves makes a compromise necessary.
There are many divided countries in the world. This afternoon one member mentioned Cyprus. British Guiana is another country in which there is strife. There is also strife in the Middle East, and considerable strife in our neighbouring country to the south, but if the cards are on the table surely we as grown men and women should be able to compromise, to sit down in a committee of 10 or 11-it does not matter how many-to go into it with the sole purpose of coming out with a solution, and be prepared to compromise. Surely in such a committee we could arrive at a suitable flag, whether it has one maple leaf or three, whether it has the union jack or not. Surely we have reached the stage in this debate where we know a compromise is necessary.
I always thought the Prime Minister was a great diplomat, and I have been told that diplomacy is the art of compromise. I only hope some of that diplomacy could rub off in this house so that we could take action toward a compromise. The committee in 1945 which studied this flag question had something like 2,400 designs presented to it and I believe the members of that committee really considered this problem and worked on it. They tried to reach a decision which all Canada would accept and honour. Some 25 members approved the recommendations of the committee and one was opposed. I think this represented a tremendous effort on the part of that committee to reach a solution. Perhaps the same could be accomplished at the present time.
This should have been taken into account by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) before he put forward his three maple leaf design and said: Accept this, or else. This issue has been talked about for so many years in Canada that it should have been realized, particularly by those on the government side, that if the committee to which I have referred could not reach a conclusion, the matter ought now to be placed in the form of a referendum and sent to the people for decision. I am not saying this should be done immediately. But it might be done whenever the next election is held. There would be no significant extra cost about asking Canadian citizens to make two X's on ballot forms, one in relation to the election and the other with regard to their flag preference. This would constitute a relatively simple solution to this problem and I think it is the solution which all Canadians would accept. In addition, it

would not take nearly so much of the time of this house to ratify the result of such a plebiscite. An amendment and a subamendment have been moved. In the subamendment, four suggestions have been put forward. I think a flag is something which should embody our tradition and history, a symbol which all Canadians are prepared to accept. If it is evident that any major portion of our country is not prepared to accept the symbol put forward by the government, or by parliament, we should have enough common sense not to press the suggestion.
Hear, hear.

I am glad an hon. member on the other side agrees with me. We should be prepared to bring forward a design which will be generally accepted and which will unite the country-a flag which every Canadian will be proud to honour.
Not long ago I met an old schoolteacher of mine, and while renewing acquaintance he told me he had been teaching for three years in Europe. While I was not his favourite pupil in school-we had our disagreements in those days-I found we got along fairly well, meeting outside in the hurly-burly of life. I told him what we were engaged in at the moment -the flag debate in parliament and he told me he had travelled all across Europe during the summer recess. He had visited all the points of interest to Canadians; he had seen the crosses on many of the war graves over there. And he said to me: The red ensign is accepted as the Canadian symbol in Europe. I might add that this teacher is neither French nor English in origin. He told me he shuddered to think that any government was
Canadian Flag prepared, so callously, to wipe out the past and do away with the symbol of freedom for which these men fought and died. His parting words were: Do not let that government bring in this three maple leaf flag without first submitting it to the people-without first getting unanimous support from the people, because the symbol of a country without the people behind it means very little. These are the words he spoke to me recently and I cannot help but remember them and put them before the house.
Surely we must be prepared as legislators to bring in a flag which means something to everybody-a flag which can be recognized and honoured by everybody. We are grown men and women and are able to sit down in a committee and discuss this matter. And if a solution cannot be found in a committee, then surely it could be reached along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More). In any event, the committee could decide on a list of questions to be inserted in a plebiscite and the people could then choose which flag they wish to honour in the years ahead.
I am sure Canadians do not want a flag which was picked by one man, rammed down the throat of parliament by a government which in this connection has little regard for freedom of thought and freedom of speech. Fear of being deprived of a recess was held over our heads; we were told that if we did not pass this motion we would have no recess. I am proud of being a member of the party which puts duty first and a recess last.
May I call it 10.30?
At 10.30 p.m. the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to special order.

Tuesday, August 25, 1964
